title: Credit Card Payoff Calculator - How Long to Pay Off Your Card and Total Interest
html:
Credit Card Payoff Calculator

Card balance
$
APR
%
How do you want to pay it off?
Monthly payment
$
Months to pay off
months

Assumes no new purchases and a fixed APR. Interest is charged monthly at APR ÷ 12.

Credit card interest is one of the most expensive debts there is. Paying only the minimum can stretch a balance out for many years. Use this calculator to see exactly when you will be debt-free and how much interest you will pay.

Why paying a little more changes everything

Credit card interest is charged on the balance you carry each month. At typical rates above 20%, a payment that only slightly exceeds the interest barely moves the balance. That is why the minimum payment can keep you in debt for years. This calculator shows how long payoff takes and how much interest you pay at the amount you choose.

How to use the credit card payoff calculator

  1. Enter your current balance and APR.
  2. Choose a fixed monthly payment, or a target number of months.
  3. Press Calculate to see your payoff date and total interest.

The formula

Each month: new balance = balance + balance × (APR ÷ 12) − payment

Worked example: $6,000 at 22.99% APR

Monthly paymentTime to pay offTotal interest
$150≈ 77 months (6.4 years)≈ $5,490
$300≈ 26 months≈ $1,640

Doubling the payment cuts the time by about two-thirds and saves around $3,850. If $300 is not possible, even $200 makes a large difference — try it in the calculator.

The 36-month figure on your statement, decoded

Since the Credit CARD Act of 2009, nearly every statement must show how long payoff takes at the minimum and, unless that is already under three years, the monthly amount that clears the balance in 36 months. That box is a ready-made target you can test here.

Take a $4,000 balance at 24% APR. A typical minimum is interest plus 1% of the balance, about $120 at first. Paying a flat $120 every month takes roughly 56 months and costs about $2,660 in interest. The statement's 36-month figure works out to about $157 a month, with total interest near $1,650. That extra $37 a month cuts 20 months off the payoff and saves about $1,000.

To check your own statement, enter 36 in the months field and compare the payment returned. Both the statement box and this tool assume no new charges and a fixed APR.

A plan that works

  1. Stop adding new charges to the card you are paying off. Use a debit card for daily spending.
  2. Pick a fixed payment you can keep every month, and set up automatic payment.
  3. Call the issuer and ask for a lower APR. Customers with on-time history are sometimes offered one.
  4. Consider a 0% balance transfer if you can pay it off before the promotion ends. Watch the transfer fee (often 3–5%).
  5. Several cards? Use the snowball or avalanche method to choose which card gets the extra money.

Common mistakes

  • Paying the minimum, which usually shrinks as the balance shrinks — stretching payoff even further.
  • Moving debt to a 0% card and then running the old card back up.
  • Closing old cards right away; it can raise your credit utilization ratio and lower your score.

Myth versus fact on credit card interest

  • Myth: carrying a small balance helps your credit score. Fact: scores reward a low balance relative to your limit on the statement date; paying in full costs you nothing in score terms.
  • Myth: only the old balance accrues interest. Fact: once you carry a balance, most issuers suspend the grace period, so new purchases accrue interest from the day you make them.
  • Myth: the minimum payment is a fixed percentage. Fact: it is usually interest and fees plus about 1% of principal, or a floor such as $25 to $35, whichever is greater, which is why it shrinks as the balance falls.
  • Myth: a 0% balance transfer is free. Fact: the transfer fee of 3% to 5% is added to the balance up front, $180 to $300 on a $6,000 transfer. It often still beats a 22% APR.
  • Myth: every 0% promotion works the same way. Fact: deferred interest offers, common on store cards, charge all the interest back from day one if any balance remains when the promotion ends. A true 0% intro APR does not.

Reader questions about paying down a card balance

How is credit card interest calculated?
Most issuers use the average daily balance and a daily rate (APR ÷ 365). This calculator uses a monthly rate (APR ÷ 12), which gives very close results.

Does paying twice a month help?
Slightly, because the average daily balance is lower. The bigger win is the total amount you pay each month.

Should I pay off cards before saving?
Most planners suggest a small emergency fund first (so new emergencies don't go on the card), then aggressive payoff of high-interest debt.

Why does the minimum payment take so long?
Minimum payments are often about 1–3% of the balance, so most of the payment goes to interest and the balance falls slowly.

Should I pay off the highest APR card first?
Paying the highest APR first (the avalanche method) saves the most money. Try our Debt Payoff Calculator to compare methods.

Debt Snowball vs Avalanche · Loan Calculator · Compound Interest

Sources and further reading

  • Federal Reserve – consumer credit card rules and disclosure requirements

title: Age Calculator - How Old Am I in Years, Months and Days?
html:
Age Calculator

Date of birth
Age on this date (today is pre-selected)

Counts calendar years, months and days.

How old are you exactly — to the day? This calculator shows your age in years, months and days, how many days you have lived, the day of the week you were born, and how long until your next birthday.

How exact age is counted

Your age in years changes on your birthday, but age in months and days needs a rule, because months have different lengths. This calculator counts complete years first, then complete months, then the remaining days — the same way most forms and official documents do.

How to use the age calculator

  1. Choose your date of birth.
  2. Leave the second date as today, or choose any other date.
  3. Press Calculate Age.

The formula

Age = years and months between the dates, then the remaining days

Worked example

Someone born on June 15, 1990 is, on November 14, 2026: 36 complete years (June 15, 2026 was the 36th birthday), plus 4 complete months (to October 15), plus 30 days (October 15 to November 14). Result: 36 years, 4 months, 30 days.

Milestone birthdays measured in days, weeks and hours

The table uses the average calendar year of 365.2425 days. Your own count may differ by a day or two depending on how many February 29ths fall inside your lifetime, which is exactly what the calculator above works out for your real dates.

BirthdayDays (approx.)WeeksHours
186,574939157,785
217,6701,096184,082
3010,9571,565262,975
4014,6102,087350,633
5018,2622,609438,291
6523,7413,392569,778

Two round-number days worth marking: your 20,000th day arrives at about 54 years and 9 months, and your 25,000th at about 68 years and 5 months.

Where exact age matters

  • Benefits and retirement – Social Security full retirement age is 67 for people born in 1960 or later; you can claim from 62 with a reduced benefit.
  • Medicare – eligibility generally begins at 65.
  • School enrollment – many districts set a cut-off date for kindergarten age.
  • Insurance and licenses – driver's licenses, car insurance rates and some travel rules depend on exact age.

Leap-year birthdays

If you were born on February 29, your birthday falls on that date only every four years. For legal purposes, many U.S. states treat March 1 as the birthday in common years, while some other countries use February 28. The calculator follows the calendar strictly and shows both the years and the days.

Fun facts you can check

  • You reach 10,000 days old at about 27 years and 4 months.
  • 1 billion seconds is about 31.7 years.

Worth knowing

  • Use a future date to find how old you will be at an event.

The month-end problem: August 31 to September 30

Imagine someone born on August 31, 2000. On September 30, 2026 they have clearly lived 26 complete years. But how many months since August 31? September has no 31st, so one tool reports 26 years, 1 month, 0 days (treating the 30th as the matching day) while another reports 26 years, 0 months, 30 days. Both are defensible. The same thing happens, in some months of every year, to anyone born on the 29th, 30th or 31st.

This is why documents that depend on age almost always use whole years, and why total days lived is the one number every calculator agrees on. If you need a months figure for a form, check how that agency counts.

One rule catches people out: for Social Security, you are treated as reaching an age on the day before your birthday. Someone born on the 1st of a month is therefore considered to attain age 62 in the previous month, which can move their earliest eligible month of benefits earlier.

Things readers ask about counting their age

Does time zone matter?
For age in days, no. Age changes at midnight local time on your birthday.

Why do different calculators disagree by a day?
Some count the end date as a full day and some don't. This calculator does not count the start date, which is the usual convention.

How many days old am I?
The result shows total days lived — a fun number to celebrate, like your 10,000th day (about 27.4 years).

Why does age by year differ in some countries?
Some countries traditionally counted age differently, but international age is counted from birth as shown here.

Related calculators

Date Calculator · Retirement Calculator

Sources and further reading

  • Social Security Administration – Retirement benefits and age rules
  • U.S. Naval Observatory – Astronomical Applications (calendar and date data)

How we checked this page: the example was counted on a calendar. Background reading: Social Security Administration retirement age information (ssa.gov). Last reviewed November 2026. Age results depend on the counting convention described above and should be confirmed against official records for legal or benefits purposes.

title: ML to OZ Converter - Milliliters to Fluid Ounces (US and UK)
html:
ML to OZ Converter

Convert
Value

US fluid ounce = 29.5735 ml; UK (imperial) fluid ounce = 28.4131 ml.

Bottle labels, baby formula, recipes and skincare often mix milliliters and ounces. Convert between them instantly, in US or UK fluid ounces.

Milliliters and fluid ounces: US vs UK

A fluid ounce measures volume, and there are two of them: the US fluid ounce (29.5735 ml) and the UK imperial fluid ounce (28.4131 ml). Most American labels and recipes use the US ounce.

How to use the ml to oz converter

  1. Choose the direction.
  2. Enter the amount.
  3. Press Convert.

The formula

US fl oz = ml ÷ 29.5735  |  ml = US fl oz × 29.5735

Worked examples

  • A 500 ml water bottle = 500 ÷ 29.5735 = 16.9 US fl oz.
  • An 8 fl oz cup of coffee = 8 × 29.5735 = 236.6 ml.
  • A 2-liter soda bottle = about 67.6 US fl oz.
  • A 120 ml baby bottle feed = about 4.06 fl oz.
MeasureUSUK (imperial)
1 fluid ounce29.57 ml28.41 ml
1 pint16 fl oz = 473 ml20 fl oz = 568 ml
1 quart946 ml1,137 ml
1 gallon3.785 L4.546 L

That is why a pint of beer in a British pub (568 ml) is noticeably bigger than an American pint (473 ml).

Standard U.S. drink sizes converted to milliliters

The Dietary Guidelines for Americans define one standard drink as 12 fluid ounces of regular beer, 5 fluid ounces of wine or 1.5 fluid ounces of distilled spirits. Bottles, however, are sold in metric sizes, so the conversion decides how many servings you actually have.

Serving or containerConvertedWhat it holds
1.5 oz shot44 mlone standard drink of spirits
5 oz wine pour148 mlone standard drink of wine
12 oz can of beer355 mlone standard drink of beer
750 ml wine bottle25.4 ozabout five 5-oz pours
1.75 L spirits bottle59.2 ozabout 39 shots of 1.5 oz
2 L soda bottle67.6 ozabout 5.6 cans of 12 oz

A generous 6-ounce restaurant pour is 177 ml, more than a fifth of the bottle, so a 750 ml bottle gives only four of them.

Cups and spoons

  • 1 US cup = 8 fl oz = 236.6 ml (nutrition labels round it to 240 ml).
  • 1 tablespoon = 14.8 ml; 1 teaspoon = 4.9 ml.

Common mistakes

  • Confusing fluid ounces with weight ounces: 8 fl oz of honey weighs about 12 oz.
  • Using a UK recipe with US cups: check which country the recipe comes from.
  • Air-travel limits: the 3.4 oz rule is really 100 ml; the container size counts, not how full it is.

When the US and UK difference matters

For a single glass of water the difference between US and UK ounces is tiny, but it adds up in larger amounts. A 20-ounce British pint is about 95 ml more than a 16-ounce American pint. Recipes from Britain, Australia or older cookbooks may use imperial measures.

Medicine and baby formula deserve extra care: use the measuring cup, syringe or scoop that comes with the product rather than converting in your head, and follow the label or your doctor’s directions.

Quick reminders

  • TSA carry-on liquid limit: 3.4 oz (100 ml) per container.

The 64-ounce day in bottles and liters

The familiar advice to drink eight 8-ounce glasses adds up to 64 fl oz, or 1.89 liters. In the 16.9-ounce (500 ml) bottles sold in packs, that is 3.8 bottles. A 32-ounce refillable bottle (946 ml) needs two fills. A 1-liter bottle holds 33.8 ounces, so two of them is slightly more than the 64-ounce target.

The eight-glasses figure is a rule of thumb rather than an official standard. The Dietary Guidelines recommend water as the main beverage but set no glass count, and water from food, coffee and other drinks also counts toward intake. Needs rise with heat and exercise.

Going the other way, a European label that says 2 L a day means 67.6 ounces, about eight and a half 8-ounce glasses. For any amount in this range, the US-UK difference is about 4%: 64 US fl oz is 1,893 ml, while 64 imperial fl oz is 1,818 ml.

Readers' questions on milliliters and ounces

How many ounces should a newborn drink?
Feeding amounts vary by baby and age; follow your pediatrician’s advice. This page only converts units.

Is 1 liter more than a quart?
Yes, slightly: 1 L = 33.8 US fl oz, and a US quart is 32 fl oz.

How many ml in 1 oz?
One US fluid ounce is 29.57 ml; one UK fluid ounce is 28.41 ml.

How many oz in 1 liter?
About 33.8 US fluid ounces.

Related calculators

Calorie Calculator · Percentage Calculator · Tip Calculator

Sources and further reading

  • Dietary Guidelines for Americans – standard drink sizes and beverage guidance
  • NIST Office of Weights and Measures – U.S. customary and metric volume units

title: CM to Inches Converter - Centimeters to Inches and Feet (Height Chart)
html:
CM to Inches Converter

Convert
Value

1 inch = 2.54 cm exactly.

Convert centimeters to inches — and to feet and inches for height — or go the other way. Great for clothing sizes, screens, furniture and international recipes.

Centimeters and inches in everyday life

Since 1959 one inch has been defined as exactly 2.54 centimeters, so the conversion never changes — only the rounding does. This converter shows inches, feet and inches, and the nearest 1/16 inch for tape-measure work.

How to use the cm to inches converter

  1. Choose the direction.
  2. Enter the value.
  3. Press Convert.

The formula

inches = cm ÷ 2.54  |  cm = inches × 2.54

Worked examples

  • Height: 170 cm ÷ 2.54 = 66.93 in = 5 ft 6.9 in.
  • The other way: 5 ft 10 in = 70 in × 2.54 = 177.8 cm.
  • A 55-inch TV measures 55 × 2.54 = 139.7 cm diagonally (the screen, not the frame).
  • Jeans with a 32-inch waist are 81.3 cm around.
InchesCentimetersWhere you see it
12 in (1 ft)30.48 cmRulers, floor tiles
24 in60.96 cmKitchen counter depth
32 in81.28 cmWaist sizes, small TVs
36 in (1 yd)91.44 cmFabric, door widths
55 in139.7 cmTV screens
65 in165.1 cmTV screens

Paper and photo sizes: A-series versus U.S. inches

Most of the world prints on A4; the United States uses Letter. They are close enough to confuse and different enough to cut off a margin, and photo frames sold in centimeters have the same problem.

SizeCentimetersInches
A421.0 x 29.7 cm8.27 x 11.69 in
US Letter21.59 x 27.94 cm8.5 x 11 in
A329.7 x 42.0 cm11.69 x 16.54 in
Tabloid (Ledger)27.94 x 43.18 cm11 x 17 in
4 x 6 photo10.16 x 15.24 cmsold abroad as 10 x 15 cm
8 x 10 photo20.32 x 25.4 cmsold abroad as 20 x 25 cm

A4 is 0.23 inches narrower and 0.69 inches taller than Letter, which is why a document from Europe loses its top or bottom line unless you choose fit to page. A 4 x 6 print is 1.6 mm wider and 2.4 mm taller than a 10 x 15 cm frame opening, so it may need a trim.

Quick mental math

  • 10 cm is a little under 4 inches (3.94 in).
  • 30 cm is about one foot (11.8 in).
  • For a rough cm → in estimate, multiply by 4 and divide by 10: 50 cm ≈ 20 in (exact: 19.7 in).

Common mistakes

  • Writing 5.6 ft for 5 ft 6 in — 5.6 ft is 5 ft 7.2 in.
  • Rounding too early: convert first, then round at the end.
  • Measuring screens across the frame: TV and monitor sizes are the visible diagonal only.

When people need this conversion

Online shopping is the most common reason: furniture, rugs, luggage and clothing from other countries often list only centimeters or only inches. Doctors’ offices, passports and sports profiles may ask for height in a different unit than you are used to.

For anything that must fit — a sofa through a doorway, a TV in a cabinet, a carry-on in an overhead bin — convert the exact measurement and leave a little extra room. Product dimensions are usually rounded, and packaging adds size.

Moving-day checklist for metric furniture

Common U.S. interior doors are 30 or 32 inches wide (76.2 or 81.3 cm); exterior doors are usually 36 inches (91.4 cm). Suppose a sofa from a European retailer is listed as 220 x 90 x 78 cm.

  1. Convert every dimension: 86.6 x 35.4 x 30.7 inches.
  2. Compare the two smallest dimensions with the door. The 35.4-inch depth will not pass a 32-inch door upright, but tipped on its side the 30.7-inch height clears with 1.3 inches to spare.
  3. Measure the clear opening with the door open, not the door slab; the frame, stops and hinges take back an inch or more.
  4. Walk the route: hallway width, stair landings and the elevator door.
  5. Allow for packaging. Shipping cartons add several centimeters, so unbox at the door if the margin is thin.
  6. Check whether the legs unscrew; removing them reduces the height dimension that matters when the sofa goes through sideways.

Common questions about cm and inches

How many centimeters are in a foot?
30.48 cm exactly.

Why does my clothing label show both?
International brands list both; small differences come from sizing systems, not the conversion.

How many inches is 1 cm?
1 cm = 0.3937 inches.

How tall is 5 ft 10 in in cm?
5 ft 10 in = 70 inches × 2.54 = 177.8 cm.

Related calculators

BMI Calculator · Percentage Calculator · Age Calculator

Sources and further reading

  • NIST – SI units and the exact inch-to-centimeter definition
  • NIST Office of Weights and Measures – U.S. customary units

How we checked this page: every conversion was recalculated with 1 in = 2.54 cm and matched the converter. Last reviewed November 2026. Converted figures are exact but product dimensions are often rounded, so measure the item itself before buying or moving it.

Auto Loan Calculator

Car price
$

$

$
Sales tax
%

%
Loan term

Sales tax is applied to the price minus the trade-in (rules vary by state). Fees such as title and registration are not included.

Dealers love to talk about the monthly payment. This auto loan calculator shows you the whole picture — the amount financed, sales tax, total interest and what the car really costs — before you sign.

Getting the real cost of a car loan

Dealers often lead with the monthly payment, because a low number is easy to say yes to. The better way to shop is to settle the out-the-door price first — vehicle price plus sales tax, title, registration and dealer fees, minus your trade-in and down payment — and then decide how to finance that amount. This calculator follows that order so you can see each piece separately.

How to use the auto loan calculator

  1. Enter the car price, your down payment and any trade-in value.
  2. Enter your state sales tax rate.
  3. Enter the APR and choose a loan term.
  4. Press Calculate.

The formula

Amount financed = price + sales tax − down payment − trade-in

Worked example

A $35,000 car, 7% sales tax, an $8,000 trade-in and $3,000 down at 7.5% APR:

  • In states that tax the price after the trade-in, tax is charged on $27,000, and you finance about $25,890. Over 60 months that is about $519 a month.
  • In states that tax the full price, tax is charged on $35,000 and you finance about $26,450 — about $530 a month.

Most states give the trade-in tax credit, but some do not, so check your state's rule. It can make a difference of several hundred dollars.

Case study: 0% APR versus a $2,500 rebate

You are financing $30,000 over 60 months. The manufacturer offers either 0% APR or a $2,500 cash rebate, not both.

  • 0% APR: $30,000 ÷ 60 = $500 a month, total paid $30,000.
  • Rebate plus a 6.5% credit union loan: finance $27,500 at 6.5% for 60 months = $538 a month, total paid $32,284. The 0% deal wins by $2,284.
  • Rebate plus a 4.5% loan: $513 a month, total $30,761. The 0% deal still wins, by $761.

The rebate only comes out ahead when the interest on the reduced balance is less than the rebate. For these numbers that happens below roughly 3.5% APR over 60 months. Run your own quote in the calculator with the price lowered by the rebate, and remember that 0% offers usually require top-tier credit and may be limited to shorter terms.

60 vs 72 vs 84 months

$26,450 at 7.5%MonthlyWhat to watch
60 months≈ $530Balance usually falls faster than the car's value
72 months≈ $457About $1,100 more interest; higher risk of owing more than the car is worth

Being "upside down" (owing more than the car is worth) matters if the car is totaled or you want to sell early. A larger down payment, a shorter term or GAP insurance reduces that risk.

Ways to lower the cost

  • Get pre-approved by a bank or credit union before visiting the dealer, so you have a rate to compare.
  • Negotiate price, trade-in and financing separately. Combining them makes it easy to give back savings in another place.
  • Watch add-ons (extended warranties, protection packages). They are often rolled into the loan and charged interest.
  • Check the APR, not only the rate. Special 0% offers may require giving up a cash rebate — run both options.

Loan balance versus car value over a 72-month term

Being upside down depends on how fast the balance falls relative to the car's value. The table assumes a $35,000 car with 7% sales tax at 7.5% APR for 72 months, and an illustrative value drop of 20% in year one and 15% a year after that. Those value figures are assumptions, not forecasts.

MonthBalance, nothing down ($37,450 financed)Balance, $8,000 trade-in + $3,000 down ($26,450 financed)Illustrative car value
12$32,314$22,823$28,000
24$26,780$18,914$23,800
36$20,816$14,702$20,230
48$14,389$10,163$17,196

With nothing down, the buyer owes more than the car is worth for about three years, by $4,300 at the one-year mark. With $11,000 of trade-in and cash, the balance stays below the value from the start. If a zero-down loan is the only option, GAP coverage protects you during that first-three-years gap, and a shorter term closes it faster.

Car buyers' questions about loan math

How much car can I afford?
A common rule of thumb is to keep total car costs (payment, insurance, fuel) under about 15–20% of take-home pay, and the loan term at 60 months or less.

Are dealer fees included?
Add documentation, title and registration fees to the price field. They vary by state and dealer.

Is a 0% offer always best?
Not if it replaces a large rebate. Compare: 0% on the full price versus a rebate plus your own bank's rate.

Is a 72- or 84-month loan a good idea?
It lowers the payment, but you pay more interest and may be “upside down” for years. 60 months or less is usually safer.

Does the trade-in reduce sales tax?
In most US states, yes — tax is charged on the price minus the trade-in. A few states do not allow this credit.

Related calculators

Loan Calculator · Debt Snowball vs Avalanche

  • MyMoney.gov – federal financial literacy resources on borrowing

Assumes a 30-year loan, 1.1% property tax, 0.35% insurance, 1% maintenance per year, 3% buying and 6% selling costs.

Is buying always better than renting? Not necessarily. It depends on prices, interest rates and especially how long you stay. This calculator compares the net cost of both choices over your own timeline.

Renting vs buying: compare total cost, not monthly payment

A mortgage payment and a rent check look similar, but they buy different things. Part of a mortgage payment builds equity; rent does not. On the other hand, owners pay costs renters never see: property tax, insurance, maintenance, closing costs and the money tied up in the down payment, which could have been invested. This calculator adds all of these over the years you expect to stay, then compares them with the total cost of renting.

How to use the rent vs buy calculator

  1. Enter the home price, down payment and mortgage rate.
  2. Enter the rent for a similar home and how many years you will stay.
  3. Adjust price growth, rent growth and investment return.
  4. Press Compare.

The formula

Net cost of buying = all payments + taxes + upkeep + buying costs − equity when you sell

The costs people forget

  • Opportunity cost – a $60,000 down payment invested at 5% would earn about $3,000 a year.
  • Maintenance – budget about 1–2% of the home's value per year.
  • Buying and selling costs – closing costs to buy (2–5%) and agent and transfer costs to sell (often 5–8%).
  • Rent increases – rent tends to rise each year, while a fixed-rate mortgage payment doesn't.

Case study: $400,000 purchase against $2,300 rent

Using the default assumptions: 20% down ($80,000), a $320,000 loan at 6.5% for 30 years, a five-year stay, 3% home price growth, 3% rent growth and a 5% return on cash.

Buying. Principal and interest are $2,023 a month, $121,357 over five years. Property tax, insurance and maintenance (1.1% + 0.35% + 1%) add $9,800 a year, $49,000 in total. Buying costs at 3% are $12,000. Cash out: $262,357. The home grows to $463,710; after 6% selling costs and the $299,555 still owed, you walk away with $136,332. Net cost of owning: about $126,000.

Renting. Rent starts at $2,300 and rises 3% a year: $146,532 over five years. The $92,000 not spent on the down payment and closing earns 5%, growing by $25,418. Net cost of renting: about $121,100.

Renting wins by roughly $5,000, about $80 a month, a tie in practice. Raise price growth to 4% and buying wins by about $16,700; raise the rent to $2,500 and buying wins by about $7,800. Small inputs decide this one.

Why the time you stay matters most

Because buying and selling are expensive, buying usually loses over short periods. As the years go by, equity builds, rent keeps rising and the one-time costs are spread out. Many comparisons find a break-even somewhere around five years, but it varies widely with prices, rents and rates in your area. Run the calculator with your own numbers and try a few different "years you'll stay".

Non-financial factors

Owning gives control and stability — you can renovate and won't be asked to move. Renting gives flexibility, lower upfront cash and no surprise repair bills. Both are reasonable choices; the numbers just show the price of each.

Property tax: the input that varies most by state

The default 1.1% is roughly a national average, but effective property tax rates run from roughly 0.3% in Hawaii to more than 2% in New Jersey and Illinois. Texas sits well above average, while California's effective rate is below 1% because assessed values are capped until a sale.

On a $400,000 home that spread is large: 0.3% is $1,200 a year ($100 a month), 1.1% is $4,400 ($367 a month) and 2.0% is $8,000 ($667 a month). Over five years the gap between the low and high case is about $34,000, more than enough to flip the result above.

Two cautions. In many states the home is reassessed at your purchase price, so the seller's current bill understates yours. Homeowners insurance varies the same way, with coastal and wildfire areas costing far more than 0.35%. Check the county assessor's site and a real quote before trusting the defaults.

Renters and buyers ask

What home price growth should I use?
Use a modest long-run figure such as 2–4% a year, and test a lower one. Local markets can fall as well as rise.

Is rent "throwing money away"?
No. Rent buys housing and flexibility; interest, taxes and maintenance are the owner's equivalent "unrecoverable" costs.

Are tax deductions included?
Mortgage interest only helps if you itemize, which fewer households do since the standard deduction rose. The comparison is more reliable without assuming a deduction.

Why include investment return?
Money used for a down payment could otherwise be invested. Counting that lost growth makes the comparison fair.

Are the assumptions right for my area?
Property tax and insurance vary a lot by state. The defaults are national averages; your result is an estimate.

Related calculators

Mortgage Calculator · Home Affordability

title: Retirement Calculator - How Much Will I Have at Retirement? (401k, IRA, 4% Rule)
html:
Retirement Savings Calculator

Current age
years
Retirement age
years
Current retirement savings
$
Monthly contribution (including employer match)
$
Expected annual return
%
Expected inflation
%

Uses the 4% rule to estimate a sustainable first-year withdrawal. Returns are not guaranteed.

Will your 401(k), IRA and other savings be enough? This retirement calculator projects your balance at retirement, shows it in today’s dollars, and estimates the income it could support using the popular 4% rule.

Turning a retirement balance into a plan

A retirement projection has two halves: how much you may have saved by retirement, and how much income that balance can safely provide. This calculator estimates the first with compound growth and the second with the widely used 4% guideline.

How to use the retirement calculator

  1. Enter your current age and planned retirement age.
  2. Enter what you have saved and what you add each month.
  3. Adjust the expected return and inflation.
  4. Press Calculate.

The formula

Safe first-year withdrawal ≈ 4% of savings at retirement

Worked example

Age 35, $50,000 saved, $600 a month added, 6% average return until 65. The projection is about $904,000. Using the 4% guideline, that could support roughly $36,000 a year in the first year of retirement, adjusted for inflation after that — before Social Security or any pension.

Remember that $904,000 in 30 years will buy less than it does today. At 3% inflation, it is worth about $370,000 in today's dollars. Look at the inflation-adjusted figure when you judge whether it is enough.

2026 contribution limits and the new Roth catch-up rule

For 2026 the IRS limit on employee deferrals to a 401(k), 403(b) or most 457 plans is $24,500. Workers 50 and older can add a catch-up of $8,000, and those aged 60 to 63 may contribute a higher catch-up of $11,250 if their plan allows it. The IRA limit is $7,500, with a $1,100 catch-up at 50 and over.

New this year under the SECURE 2.0 Act: catch-up contributions from workers whose prior-year wages from that employer exceeded about $150,000 must go into a Roth (after-tax) account. If the plan has no Roth option, those workers cannot make catch-ups at all, so check with your plan administrator.

To see the ceiling in the calculator, enter $2,042 a month for the base limit ($24,500 ÷ 12) or $2,708 with the standard catch-up, then add any employer match on top; the match does not count against the employee limit.

What the 4% guideline means

It comes from studies of historical U.S. market returns, which found that withdrawing about 4% in the first year and raising the amount with inflation lasted around 30 years in most past periods. It is a starting point, not a guarantee; longer retirements or poor early returns may call for a lower rate.

Ways to improve the result

  • Capture the employer match in a 401(k) — it's often the best return you can get.
  • Raise contributions by 1% each year or each time you get a raise.
  • Use tax-advantaged accounts (401(k), IRA, Roth IRA) for tax-deferred or tax-free growth.
  • Work a little longer – it adds contributions, adds growth and shortens the years you need to fund.

Social Security at 62, 67 or 70: one benefit, three sizes

For anyone born in 1960 or later, full retirement age is 67. Claiming early reduces the benefit by 5/9 of 1% per month for the first 36 months and 5/12 of 1% for each month beyond that; waiting past 67 adds 8% a year until 70. On a $2,000 full-age benefit:

Claiming ageShare of full benefitMonthly amount
6270%$1,400
6480%$1,600
6586.7%$1,733
67100%$2,000
68108%$2,160
70124%$2,480

Ignoring cost-of-living adjustments, the person who waits until 70 catches up with the one who claimed at 62 at around age 80. Add your chosen figure to the 4% income the calculator shows for a fuller picture of retirement cash flow.

Retirement planning questions answered

How much do I need?
A common estimate is 70–80% of pre-retirement income, from all sources combined.

What return should I enter?
Use a conservative figure (for example 5–6% for a balanced portfolio) and test a lower one to see the range.

Is Social Security included?
No. Check your estimate at ssa.gov and add it to the income from savings.

What is the 4% rule?
Research found that withdrawing 4% of savings in the first year, then adjusting for inflation, historically lasted about 30 years in most cases.

How much do I need to retire?
A common guideline is 25 times your expected yearly spending, or 70–80% of your pre-retirement income.

Related calculators

Sources and further reading

title: Refinance Calculator - Monthly Savings and Break-Even Point for a Mortgage Refinance
html:
Mortgage Refinance Calculator

Current loan balance
$
Current interest rate
%
Years left on current loan
years
New interest rate
%
New loan term
Closing costs
$

Compares principal and interest only. Closing costs are assumed to be paid up front, not rolled into the loan.

Refinancing can lower your payment when rates drop, but closing costs mean it only pays off if you stay long enough. This calculator shows your monthly savings and how many months it takes to break even.

Is refinancing worth it? Look at the break-even point

Refinancing replaces your current mortgage with a new one, usually to get a lower rate, change the term or take cash out. It is never free: closing costs commonly run 2–5% of the loan. The key question is how many months of lower payments it takes to earn those costs back. That is the break-even point, and this calculator shows it directly.

How to use the refinance calculator

  1. Enter your current balance, rate and years left.
  2. Enter the new rate and term you were offered.
  3. Enter the estimated closing costs.
  4. Press Should I Refinance?

The formula

Break-even months = closing costs ÷ monthly savings

Worked example

You owe $300,000 at 7% with 28 years left; your payment is about $2,039. A new 30-year loan at 6% would be about $1,799 — roughly $240 a month less. With $6,000 in closing costs, break-even is about 25 months. If you plan to stay at least three years, the refinance probably pays off.

Be careful: starting a new 30-year clock adds two years of payments. If you choose a new loan that matches your remaining 28 years, the payment is about $1,845 — still $194 less — and you don't extend your debt.

Case study: refinancing $300,000 into a 15-year loan

You owe $300,000 at 7% with 28 years left: $2,039 a month and about $385,000 of interest still to pay. Shorter loans usually carry lower rates (Freddie Mac publishes 15-year and 30-year averages weekly), so the illustrative rates below step down with the term.

OptionMonthly P&IRemaining interestInterest saved
Keep current loan (28 yrs, 7%)$2,039$385,045-
New 30-year at 6%$1,799$347,515$37,500, but two extra years
New 20-year at 6.25%$2,193$226,268$158,800
New 15-year at 5.75%$2,491$148,421$236,600

The 15-year loan costs $452 more a month and finishes 13 years sooner, saving about $237,000. The break-even formula does not apply when the payment rises, so judge it on total interest and on whether the higher payment fits your budget with room to spare.

When refinancing usually makes sense

  • The new rate is meaningfully lower (often 0.75–1 point or more) and you'll stay past break-even.
  • You want to drop PMI after your home has risen in value.
  • You want to move from an adjustable rate to a fixed rate before it resets.
  • You want a shorter term to pay the house off sooner.

When it often doesn't

  • You may sell or move before break-even.
  • You're far into the loan and most of each payment already goes to principal.
  • The "no-cost" offer simply adds the costs to the rate or balance — compare the APR.

Six numbers to check on every Loan Estimate

Lenders must give you a Loan Estimate within three business days of your application, and the form is standardized so offers line up.

  1. Rate and rate lock. Confirm the rate is locked and for how many days; an expired lock can cost you the quoted rate.
  2. Section A, origination charges. This is the lender's own fee and the cleanest line to compare between lenders.
  3. Points. One point is 1% of the loan, $3,000 on $300,000. Divide the cost of the points by the monthly saving they create to get their own break-even.
  4. Rolled-in costs. If $6,000 of costs is added to the 30-year 6% loan above, the payment becomes $1,835 instead of $1,799, and the monthly saving falls from $240 to $204 for the life of the loan.
  5. Prepayment penalty. The yes-or-no box on page one should say No if you plan to pay extra or sell early.
  6. Cash to close. Prepaid interest and the new escrow deposit are not lender fees, but they are real cash due at closing, partly offset later by the refund of your old escrow balance.

Homeowners' questions about refinancing

Should I pay points?
Points lower the rate in exchange for cash now. Divide the cost of the points by the monthly saving they create to find their own break-even.

Does refinancing hurt my credit?
The credit check causes a small, temporary dip. Shopping several lenders within a short window is usually treated as one inquiry.

Is cash-out refinancing a good idea?
It can fund major repairs at a low rate, but it turns home equity into debt secured by your house.

How much does the rate need to drop?
A common rule of thumb is about 0.75–1 percentage point, but the break-even calculation is more reliable.

What are typical closing costs?
Often 2–5% of the loan amount, including appraisal, title and lender fees.

Related calculators

Mortgage Calculator · Home Affordability

Sources and further reading

  • Consumer Financial Protection Bureau – Mortgages: refinancing and the Loan Estimate
  • Freddie Mac – Primary Mortgage Market Survey (15-year and 30-year average rates)
  • Consumer Financial Protection Bureau – Owning a Home: comparing loan offers

How we checked this page: payments recomputed with the amortization formula; break-even = closing costs ÷ monthly saving. Background reading: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau refinancing guidance. Last reviewed November 2026. Refinance savings shown are illustrative; actual rates, fees and tax effects differ, so review a Loan Estimate with your lender before deciding.

title: How Many Weeks Left in the Year? Today’s Date, Week Number and Day of Year
html:
Today’s Date & Weeks Left in the Year

Or check another date

Week numbers follow the ISO 8601 standard (weeks start on Monday).

How many weeks are left this year? What week number is it? The box at the top updates automatically every day with today’s date, the ISO week number, the day of the year and the countdown to New Year.

Counting down the rest of the year

Knowing exactly how many days and weeks remain helps with year-end goals, savings targets and holiday planning. The live box updates every day; you can also check any other date.

How to use the weeks left in the year

  1. Look at the live box for today.
  2. To check another date, choose it below and press Calculate.

The formula

Days left = days in the year − day of the year  |  weeks left = days left ÷ 7

Worked example: November 14, 2026

November 14 is day 318 of 2026, which has 365 days. That leaves 47 days — 6 weeks and 5 days — until December 31. It falls in ISO week 46.

53 Thursdays: what a long year means for weekly paychecks

2026 starts on a Thursday and ends on a Thursday. A 365-day year is 52 weeks plus one day, so whichever weekday falls on January 1 shows up 53 times instead of 52. In 2026 that weekday is Thursday.

Anyone paid every Thursday therefore receives 53 paychecks this year instead of the usual 52. Anyone paid every other Thursday may receive 27 checks instead of 26, depending on where their cycle falls. Employers handle this in different ways: some divide a fixed salary into 27 slightly smaller checks, some pay one extra check, and hourly workers are simply paid for the extra hours. If a benefit premium is deducted from every check, ask payroll whether the extra check is treated differently.

The same quirk is why the ISO calendar gives 2026 a week 53: the week of December 28 to January 3 has its Thursday (December 31) in 2026, so it counts as week 53 of 2026 rather than week 1 of 2027.

What is an ISO week number?

Under the ISO 8601 standard, weeks start on Monday and week 1 is the week that contains the year’s first Thursday. Because of that rule, some years have 53 weeks. 2026 is one of them: it starts on a Thursday, so December 28–31, 2026 belong to week 53.

YearDaysISO weeks
202536552
202636553
202736552
2028 (leap year)36652

Ways to use the countdown

  • Savings goals: divide what you still need by the weeks left. $940 to go with 47 days left is about $140 a week.
  • Year-end work: count business weeks rather than calendar weeks, and remember the holidays.
  • Habits: a daily habit started today runs 47 times before New Year.

Common mistakes

  • Assuming every year has 52 weeks — ISO years can have 53.
  • Mixing week systems: US calendars often start weeks on Sunday, which can shift the week number.

Planning with weeks instead of months

Weeks are handy for planning because they always have seven days, while months vary from 28 to 31. Teachers count weeks left in a semester, project managers plan in weekly sprints, and many workplaces track goals by week number.

If you share week numbers with people in other countries, say which system you use. The ISO system starts weeks on Monday, while many US calendars start on Sunday, which can move a date into a different week.

Case study: 37 days, 25 working days and a $1,200 holiday budget

Take Tuesday, November 24, 2026. It is day 328 of the year and falls in ISO week 48. That leaves 37 days, or 5 weeks and 2 days, until December 31.

Those 37 days contain 27 weekdays. Subtract Thanksgiving (Thursday, November 26) and Christmas (Friday, December 25) and you have 25 working days. If your office also closes on the Friday after Thanksgiving, make it 24.

  • Saving $1,200 for the holidays works out to $240 for each of the 5 Fridays left, or about $32 a day.
  • Paid every two weeks, you will see only two or three more checks this year, so the target is $400 to $600 per check.
  • A project that needs 60 hours of focused work needs 2.4 hours on each of those 25 working days, before any time off.

Counting in days, not months, is what makes these targets realistic.

Reader questions about week numbers and the year-end countdown

Is today counted as a day left?
No. Days left counts the days after today through December 31.

When is the next leap year?
2028. February will have 29 days and the year 366 days.

How many weeks are in a year?
52 weeks plus 1 day (2 days in a leap year). Some years have 53 ISO weeks.

What is the ISO week number?
An international standard where weeks start on Monday and week 1 contains the first Thursday of the year.

Related calculators

Days Between Dates · Age Calculator · Hours Calculator

Sources and further reading

  • U.S. Naval Observatory – Astronomical Applications (calendar and date data)
  • U.S. Department of Labor – Overtime pay (definition of the workweek)

title: Tip Calculator - How Much to Tip and Split the Bill
html:
Tip Calculator

Bill amount
$
Tip
Custom tip
%
Split between
people

In the US, tipping 15–20% of the pre-tax bill is common at sit-down restaurants.

Figure out the tip and split the check in seconds — no mental math at the table. Choose a tip percentage, enter how many people are paying, and you are done.

How much to tip — and how to split it fairly

Tipping customs in the United States are generous by world standards, because many service workers depend on tips for most of their income. This calculator works out the tip, the total and each person's share, and lets you round up so nobody has to deal with cents.

How to use the tip calculator

  1. Enter the bill amount.
  2. Choose a tip percentage or enter your own.
  3. Enter how many people are splitting the bill.
  4. Press Calculate Tip.

The formula

Tip = bill × tip %  |  each person = (bill + tip) ÷ people

Worked example

A dinner bill of $86.00 with an 18% tip: the tip is $15.48 and the total is $101.48. Split four ways, that's $25.37 each. Rounded up to $26 each, the table pays $104, which is a tip of about 21%.

Why the law lets restaurants pay servers $2.13 an hour

U.S. tipping feels mandatory because, for many servers, it is most of their pay. Under the federal Fair Labor Standards Act an employer may pay a tipped employee a cash wage of $2.13 an hour and count up to $5.12 in tips toward the $7.25 federal minimum wage. If tips fall short in a pay period, the employer must make up the difference, but the baseline the law guarantees is still $7.25.

States differ. Many set a higher cash wage for tipped workers, and several, including California, Oregon and Washington, do not allow a tip credit at all, so servers there earn the full state minimum before tips. Your 20% means something different in each place, but it is still customary everywhere.

One more legal wrinkle: a mandatory service charge printed on the bill is not a tip under federal rules. It belongs to the business unless the business chooses to pass it on. If you want to be sure the server gets something, ask whether the charge is shared, or leave a small extra amount in cash.

Typical U.S. tipping guide

ServiceCommon tip
Sit-down restaurant15–20% (18–20% is common today)
Bartender$1–2 per drink or 15–20% of the tab
Food delivery15–20%, at least $3–5
Taxi or rideshare10–20%
Hair salon / barber15–20%
Hotel housekeeping$2–5 per night

Before or after tax?

Etiquette guides usually say to tip on the pre-tax amount, though many people tip on the total for simplicity. On an $86 bill with 8% tax, the difference at 18% is only about $1.24.

Splitting when people ordered differently

An even split is simplest for friends. If one person had a much larger order, add up each person's items, apply the same tip percentage to each, and divide tax proportionally. Check the receipt for an automatic service charge — many restaurants add 18% for large groups, so you don't tip twice.

Same $64 check, four tipping choices side by side

Arguments at the table are usually about two or three percentage points. Here is what they are worth on a $64 dinner for two:

ChoiceTipTotalEach of two
15% (okay service)$9.60$73.60$36.80
18% (good)$11.52$75.52$37.76
20% (great)$12.80$76.80$38.40
25% (outstanding)$16.00$80.00$40.00
Round the total to $80$16.00$80.00$40.00

Going from 18% to 20% costs $1.28 on this bill, or 64 cents a person. The decisions that move the total more are the ones people forget: tipping on the full price of a discounted meal, and checking whether an 18% service charge was already added for your group.

Common tipping questions

Do I tip on a discounted meal?
It's considered polite to tip on the original price before the discount or coupon.

What about tipping abroad?
Customs vary widely: in Japan tipping is generally not expected, while in much of Europe a small round-up is common. Check local custom before you go.

Should I tip on the total or before tax?
Either is acceptable; tipping on the pre-tax subtotal is the traditional rule.

How much should I tip for takeout?
Tipping is optional for takeout; 10% is a kind gesture for large or complicated orders.

Related calculators

Percentage Calculator

Sources and further reading

  • U.S. Department of Labor – Minimum wage (federal rate and tipped employees)
  • Emily Post Institute – General tipping guide

title: Percent Change Calculator - Percentage Increase or Decrease Between Two Numbers
html:
Percent Change Calculator

Old value (from)
New value (to)

Percent difference compares two values without a direction, using their average.

How much did a price, salary, stock or score go up or down? Enter the old and new values to get the percent change in one click.

Reading percent change correctly

Percent change answers one question: how big was the move compared with where it started? The starting value is always the base, which is why a rise and a fall between the same two numbers give different percentages.

How to use the percent change calculator

  1. Enter the starting (old) value.
  2. Enter the ending (new) value.
  3. Press Calculate.

The formula

Percent change = (new − old) ÷ |old| × 100

Worked examples

  • Rent goes from $1,500 to $1,650: (1,650 − 1,500) ÷ 1,500 = +10%.
  • A raise from $52,000 to $55,640: 3,640 ÷ 52,000 = +7%.
  • A stock falls from $80 to $60: −20 ÷ 80 = −25%. To get back to $80 it now needs +33.3%, because the base is smaller.

Myth vs. fact: five percentage traps

  • Myth: A 20% pay cut followed by a 20% raise puts you back where you started. Fact: $100 becomes $80, then $96. You are still 4% short; the raise needed to recover is 25%.
  • Myth: Two 10% discounts equal 20% off. Fact: 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.81, so the real discount is 19%. A $200 jacket ends up at $162, not $160.
  • Myth: A price that rises 50% and then falls 50% is unchanged. Fact: $100 goes to $150, then to $75. The second move is measured from the higher base.
  • Myth: If one store's sales fall 30% and another's rise 10%, the chain is down 20%. Fact: Percentages of different-sized parts cannot be added. A $10,000 store falling 30% ($7,000) and a $30,000 store rising 10% ($33,000) total $40,000, exactly where they began.
  • Myth: A 1% monthly fee is 12% a year. Fact: 1.01 to the twelfth power is 1.1268, so the yearly cost is 12.68%.

Losses need bigger gains to recover

DropGain needed to get back to even
−10%+11.1%
−20%+25%
−25%+33.3%
−50%+100%
−75%+300%

Percent change vs. percentage points

When a mortgage rate goes from 3.5% to 4.25%, it rose by 0.75 percentage points, but the percent change is 0.75 ÷ 3.5 = +21.4%. News reports usually mean percentage points when they talk about interest rates or unemployment, so check which one is meant.

Percent change vs. percent difference

Percent difference compares two numbers without a "before" and "after", using their average as the base. For $1,500 and $1,650 the difference is 150 ÷ 1,575 = 9.52%. Use percent change for anything over time and percent difference for side-by-side comparisons, such as prices at two stores.

Changes over several years

If something grows from 100 to 150 over five years, the total change is +50%, but that is not 10% a year. The yearly (compound) rate is 1.51/5 − 1 ≈ 8.45%. For year-by-year growth use the compound interest calculator.

Common mistakes

  • Dividing by the new value instead of the old one.
  • Averaging percentages: +10% one year and −10% the next leaves you 1% lower, not even.
  • Starting from zero: a change from 0 cannot be expressed as a percent.

Everyday places you will use it

Comparing a raise with inflation, checking how much a grocery bill went up since last year, tracking a weight-loss or savings goal, and reading investment statements all use percent change. In business it shows up as month-over-month or year-over-year growth.

When you compare several changes, always use the same base period. A sales jump from a very weak month looks impressive in percent but may be small in dollars, so look at the amounts as well as the percentage.

Case study: is a 4% raise really a raise?

Suppose your salary goes from $60,000 to $62,400, a 4% increase. If prices rose 3% over the same year, the quick answer is that you came out 1% ahead. The exact answer divides instead of subtracting: 1.04 ÷ 1.03 = 1.0097, a real gain of 0.97%. In last year's dollars your new salary is worth about $60,582, so the raise bought roughly $582 of extra purchasing power, not $600.

Two habits keep this honest. First, measure both numbers over the same period; a January raise compared with a December-to-December price index covers different months. Second, look at dollars as well as percentages. A 4% raise is $2,400 on $60,000 but $1,800 on $45,000, so an across-the-board percentage raise widens the dollar gap between higher and lower earners every year it is repeated.

For the actual change in prices between two dates, use the Bureau of Labor Statistics inflation calculator rather than a remembered headline figure.

Percent change: questions that come up again and again

Can percent change be more than 100%?
Yes. Going from 50 to 150 is a 200% increase. A decrease, though, can never be more than 100%.

Is a negative result wrong?
No. A negative percent change simply means a decrease.

What is the difference between percent change and percent difference?
Percent change has a direction (old → new). Percent difference just compares two numbers using their average.

html:
Grade Calculator

What do you want to find?
AssignmentScore %Weight %
Current grade
%
Grade you want
%

%

Letter grades use the common US scale: A 90+, B 80–89, C 70–79, D 60–69, F below 60.

Want to know where you stand in a class, or what you need on the final to keep your A? Enter your scores and weights, or your current grade and final exam weight.

Working out the grade you need on the final

When a class uses weighted categories, your final grade is the weighted average of each part. That makes it possible to calculate exactly what score you need on the final exam to reach a target grade — and to know early whether a target is realistic.

How to use the grade calculator

  1. Pick “current class grade” or “what I need on the final”.
  2. Enter scores and weights from your syllabus.
  3. Press Calculate.

The formula

Weighted grade = Σ(score × weight) ÷ Σ weights  |  Final needed = (goal − current × (1 − w)) ÷ w

Worked example

Your current grade is 85% and the final exam is worth 30% of the course. To finish with 88%: (88 − 85 × 0.70) ÷ 0.30 = (88 − 59.5) ÷ 0.30 = 95% on the final. To finish with 90% you would need about 102% — not possible without extra credit, so 88% is the realistic target.

Turning a 600-point class into weights

Many syllabi never mention weights. They list points: 120 for homework, 150 for the midterm, and so on. The conversion is one division: weight = category points ÷ total points.

CategoryPoints possibleWeight
Homework12020%
Quizzes9015%
Midterm15025%
Final exam24040%
Total600100%

Points-based classes have one trap. If the syllabus drops your lowest quiz, both the points you earned and the points possible change. Four quizzes of 72, 88, 91 and 84 average 83.75%; drop the 72 and the remaining three average 87.67%, almost four points higher. Enter the drop before you plan around the number.

Weighted category example

CategoryWeightYour scoreContribution
Homework20%95%19.0
Quizzes20%80%16.0
Midterm25%78%19.5
Final35%85%29.75

Total: 19 + 16 + 19.5 + 29.75 = 84.25%.

Study tips the numbers suggest

  • A category with a large weight and a low score is where extra effort pays off most.
  • Homework points are often the easiest to secure — missing assignments can cost more than a weak quiz.
  • Check the syllabus for dropped lowest scores, curves or extra credit before assuming the worst.

Small details that change the result

  • Some teachers use a different letter scale; ask if unsure.

A six-point checklist before you set a target for the final

  1. Confirm the final's weight or point value from the syllabus, not from memory. Here, 40%.
  2. Work out your grade on everything finished so far. Say it is 83.5%.
  3. Run three targets, not one. To finish with 87% (B+) you need 92.25% on the final; to reach 90% (A-) you need 99.75%; to hold 80% (B-) you need only 74.75%.
  4. Check for a replacement policy. If the final can replace a weak midterm, the midterm's weight effectively moves into the final and the math changes.
  5. Ask how rounding works. Many instructors do not round 89.5% up to 90%, so plan for the unrounded number.
  6. Put study hours where they change the outcome. If an A- needs 99.75%, the realistic goal is the B+, and the hours saved may lift a grade in another class where the target is reachable.

Student questions about weighted grades and finals

What if weights don't add up to 100%?
Divide the weighted total by the sum of the weights entered so far to see your grade on completed work.

How do I turn a percentage into a letter grade?
Many schools use 90 = A, 80 = B, 70 = C, 60 = D, but check your course syllabus.

How is a weighted grade different from an average?
A plain average treats every score equally. A weighted grade counts each category by its share of the course.

What if my weights do not add up to 100%?
The calculator uses only the weights you entered, so it shows your grade on the work graded so far.

title: Grams to Cups Converter - Flour, Sugar, Butter and More for Baking
html:
Grams to Cups Converter

Ingredient
Convert
Amount

Approximate US cup weights for spooned-and-leveled dry ingredients. Weigh with a scale for best baking results.

A cup of flour and a cup of sugar do not weigh the same. Pick the ingredient and convert grams to cups (or cups to grams) for any recipe.

Why cups and grams don’t match

Cups measure volume and grams measure weight. A cup of flour weighs far less than a cup of honey, so every ingredient needs its own conversion. Professional bakers weigh ingredients because it is more consistent.

How to use the grams to cups converter

  1. Choose the ingredient.
  2. Choose grams → cups or cups → grams.
  3. Enter the amount and press Convert.

The formula

Cups = grams ÷ (grams per cup of that ingredient)

Worked examples

  • 250 g of flour ÷ 120 g per cup = 2.08 cups — about 2 cups plus 1 tablespoon.
  • 100 g of butter = 0.44 cup = about 7 tablespoons.
  • 1 US stick of butter = 1/2 cup = about 113 g.
  • 1 cup of granulated sugar = about 200 g.

US, metric, imperial and Japanese cups compared

Before converting grams, check whose cup the recipe means. The differences are small for a splash of milk and real for flour in bread dough.

CupVolumeWhere you meet it
US customary cup236.6 mlAmerican recipes and measuring cups; this converter
US legal cup240 mlNutrition labels on U.S. packaging
Metric cup250 mlAustralia, New Zealand, Canada and European recipes that use cups
Imperial cup284 mlOlder British recipes (10 imperial fluid ounces)
Japanese cup200 mlJapanese recipes; rice cooker cups are usually 180 ml

A metric cup holds about 5.7% more than a US cup, so a metric recipe asking for 4 cups of flour wants roughly 4 1/4 US cups. Spoons differ too: an Australian tablespoon is 20 ml, a US tablespoon about 15 ml.

How you fill the cup changes the weight

Scooping flour straight from the bag packs it down and can add 20–25% more. For the 120 g figure, spoon the flour into the cup and level it with a knife. Brown sugar is the opposite — recipes expect it packed firmly.

Ingredient1 cup1 tablespoon
All-purpose flour120 g7.5 g
Granulated sugar200 g12.5 g
Butter227 g14 g
Milk242 g15 g
Honey340 g21 g
Rolled oats89 g5.6 g

Common mistakes

  • Using one conversion for everything (such as “1 cup = 250 g”).
  • Mixing metric and US cups: a metric cup is 250 ml, a US cup is about 237 ml.
  • Converting salt like sugar: table salt is much denser — 1 cup is about 288 g.

Converting a recipe step by step

Start with the ingredients that matter most for texture — flour, sugar and butter — and convert them by weight. Small amounts such as baking soda, salt and spices can stay in teaspoons, because a kitchen scale is not precise at a few grams.

If a converted recipe turns out dry or dense, the flour was probably packed into the cup. Next time spoon it in and level it, or weigh it, and the result will match the original much more closely.

A European cake recipe converted line by line

A typical continental recipe lists 500 g flour, 250 g sugar, 200 g butter, 300 ml milk and an oven at 180 °C. Line by line:

  • 500 g all-purpose flour ÷ 120 g per cup = 4.17 cups, so 4 cups plus about 2 2/3 tablespoons, spooned and leveled.
  • 250 g granulated sugar ÷ 200 g = exactly 1 1/4 cups.
  • 200 g butter ÷ 227 g = 0.88 cup, which is 14 tablespoons, or 1 3/4 US sticks.
  • 300 ml milk ÷ 236.6 ml = 1.27 cups, so 1 1/4 cups plus a teaspoon.
  • 180 °C = 356 °F; set the oven to 350 °F.

Keep baking powder, salt and vanilla in teaspoons; a few grams is below what most kitchen scales read reliably. Eggs stay as eggs. If the result bakes dense, the flour was packed into the cup; the recipe's 500 g is the number that was right all along.

Baking conversion questions from home cooks

Is a kitchen scale worth it?
For baking, yes. Weighing removes the packing problem and makes recipes repeatable.

How many grams is a teaspoon of sugar?
About 4 g.

How many grams is 1 cup of flour?
About 120–125 g for all-purpose flour, depending on how it is measured.

Why do recipes in grams work better?
Weight does not change with packing or humidity, so results are more consistent.

title: Decimal to Fraction Calculator - Convert Decimals to Fractions and Back
html:
Decimal ↔ Fraction Converter

Convert
Decimal
Fraction
/

Decimals with up to 9 digits after the point are converted exactly.

Convert a decimal such as 0.625 into a simplified fraction (5/8), or a fraction into a decimal and percent — handy for measurements, homework and recipes.

Decimals and fractions: when each one is easier

Measurements, recipes and school math switch between decimals and fractions all the time. Decimals are easier to compare and type into a calculator; fractions match tape measures, wrenches and measuring cups. This converter goes both ways and always simplifies.

How to use the decimal to fraction calculator

  1. Choose the direction.
  2. Enter the decimal or the fraction.
  3. Press Convert.

The formula

Decimal → fraction: write it over 10, 100, 1000… then simplify (0.625 = 625/1000 = 5/8)

Worked examples

  • 0.625 = 625/1000. Divide top and bottom by 125 → 5/8.
  • 1.75 = 175/100 = 7/4 = 1 3/4.
  • 0.4 = 4/10 = 2/5.
  • 3/16 = 3 ÷ 16 = 0.1875, or 18.75%.

Fractional inch sizes and their closest metric cousins

One inch is exactly 25.4 mm, so multiply a fractional inch by 25.4 to see how close the nearest metric wrench or drill really is.

FractionDecimal inchMillimetersNearest metric size
1/40.256.356 mm (0.236 in)
3/80.3759.52510 mm (0.394 in)
7/160.437511.1111 mm (0.433 in)
1/20.512.713 mm (0.512 in)
5/80.62515.87516 mm (0.630 in)
3/40.7519.0519 mm (0.748 in)

The 3/4 inch and 19 mm pair differ by only 0.05 mm and are swapped all the time. The 1/2 inch and 13 mm pair differ by 0.3 mm, enough for the wrench to slip and round off a bolt head. To go the other way, divide millimeters by 25.4, then multiply the decimal by 16 to find the nearest sixteenth.

Reading a tape measure

Most tape measures in the U.S. are marked in sixteenths of an inch. To turn a decimal into the nearest mark, multiply the decimal part by 16 and round. For 2.3 inches: 0.3 × 16 = 4.8, which rounds to 5, so the mark is 2 5/16 inches. For metric drawings, remember 1 inch = 25.4 mm.

FractionDecimalPercent
1/80.12512.5%
1/60.166716.67%
1/50.220%
1/30.333333.33%
3/80.37537.5%
5/80.62562.5%
2/30.666766.67%
7/80.87587.5%

Repeating decimals

Some fractions never end as decimals: 1/3 = 0.333… and 1/6 = 0.1666…. If you type 0.333, the converter treats it as exactly 333/1000, because that is what you entered. When you know the value is a repeating decimal, enter the fraction (1/3) instead — that keeps your answer exact.

Common mistakes

  • Counting the wrong number of places: 0.05 is 5/100 (= 1/20), not 5/10.
  • Stopping before simplifying: 75/100 should be written as 3/4.
  • Mixing up percent and decimal: 0.5% is 0.005, not 0.5.

When converting helps most

Woodworkers and DIYers convert decimal measurements from plans or digital calipers into the nearest 1/16 or 1/32 inch on a tape. Cooks turn recipe scaling results such as 0.75 cup into 3/4 cup. Students check homework answers that must be written as simplified fractions.

A good habit is to keep full precision while you calculate and convert to a fraction only at the end. Rounding to the nearest 1/16 inch at every step can add up to a noticeable error over several cuts.

Why your timesheet says 7.75 hours, not 7:45

Payroll software stores time as decimal hours because decimals multiply cleanly by a wage. The conversion is minutes ÷ 60: 15 minutes is 0.25 hour, 20 minutes is 0.33, 45 minutes is 0.75, and 6 minutes is 0.1.

A week of 41 hours 20 minutes is 41.33 hours. For a non-exempt worker earning $18.50 an hour, that is 40 × $18.50 = $740.00 plus 1.33 overtime hours at $27.75 = $37.00, for $777.00. Type 41.20 instead of 41.33 and the check comes out $3.70 short, a small error that repeats every week.

Federal rules allow employers to round clock punches to the nearest quarter hour, as long as the rounding does not consistently favor the employer. Converting your own hours to decimals and checking them against the stub is the simplest way to catch a system that rounds the wrong way.

Decimal and fraction questions from the workshop and the classroom

How do I convert a fraction to a percent?
Divide the top by the bottom and multiply by 100. 7/8 = 0.875 = 87.5%.

What is the decimal for 1/16 inch?
0.0625 inches, which is about 1.59 mm.

Why is 0.1 + 0.2 not exactly 0.3 on some computers?
Computers store decimals in binary, which cannot represent 0.1 exactly. Fractions avoid that problem; this converter works with whole numbers internally to stay exact.

How do I convert 0.4 to a fraction?
0.4 = 4/10 = 2/5.

How do I turn a fraction into a percent?
Divide top by bottom and multiply by 100: 3/8 = 0.375 = 37.5%.

Related calculators

Percentage Calculator · Grade Calculator · Tip Calculator

Sources and further reading

  • NIST – Office of Weights and Measures (inch to millimeter definition)

  • Khan Academy – Arithmetic (fractions and decimals)

html:
Days From Today Calculator

Start date (today is pre-selected)
Number of days

What is the date 30, 60, 90 or 180 days from today? The box at the top always shows all four dates for today, and you can pick any start date and any number of days below.

30, 60, 90 and 180 days from a date

Many deadlines are written in days rather than months: a 30-day return window, net-60 invoice terms, a 90-day probation period or a 180-day warranty. This one calculator answers all of them — just change the number of days.

How to use the days from today calculator

  1. The answer for today appears automatically at the top.
  2. To use another start date or number of days, change them below.
  3. Tick “business days” to skip weekends.
  4. Press Calculate.

The formula

Date = start date + number of days (calendar days include weekends)

Example: starting Tuesday, December 1, 2026

Days addedCalendar daysBusiness days (Mon–Fri)
30Thursday, Dec 31, 2026Tuesday, Jan 12, 2027
60Saturday, Jan 30, 2027Tuesday, Feb 23, 2027
90Monday, Mar 1, 2027Tuesday, Apr 6, 2027
180Sunday, May 30, 2027Tuesday, Aug 10, 2027

Business days skip Saturdays and Sundays only. Public holidays such as Christmas or New Year’s Day are not removed, so subtract any that fall inside your period.

Deadlines written into federal consumer law

Store return windows and job probation periods are company policy. These periods are set by federal law, and each one counts a little differently:

RulePeriodHow it is counted
Dispute a credit card billing error (Fair Credit Billing Act)60 daysFrom the date the statement with the error was sent to you; the dispute must be in writing
Credit card statement to payment due date (CARD Act)21 daysAt least 21 days must pass between the statement being mailed or delivered and the due date
Cancel a refinance or home equity loan (Truth in Lending)3 business daysAfter closing; Sundays and federal holidays do not count, Saturdays do
Dispute a debt after a collector's validation notice (FDCPA)30 daysFrom the day you receive the notice, in writing
Grace period on federal Direct Loans6 monthsWritten in months, not days, after you leave school or drop below half-time

Note that a "business day" is not the same in every law: for the rescission rule a Saturday counts.

Where these numbers come up

PeriodCommon uses
30 daysReturn and refund windows, notice periods, free trials, bill due dates
60 daysNet-60 invoices, insurance and enrollment windows, two-month goals
90 daysProbation periods, quarterly plans, warranty or price-protection windows
180 daysSix-month check-ins, longer warranties, half-year savings goals

Days are not the same as months

“30 days” and “1 month” only match in some months. From January 31, 30 days later is March 2, but one month later is usually the end of February. Contracts that say “months” follow calendar months; contracts that say “days” follow this calculator.

Does the start day count?

Here the start date is day 0, so the result is the day the period ends. Some rules count the first day as day 1, which makes the deadline one day earlier. When money or legal rights are involved, read the exact wording or ask the company.

Common mistakes

  • Assuming weekends are skipped — most consumer deadlines use calendar days.
  • Forgetting holidays when you count business days.
  • Mixing time zones for online deadlines that end at midnight in a different zone.

Holidays that stretch a business-day count in early 2027

From Tuesday, December 1, 2026, 30 business days lands on Tuesday, January 12, 2027, skipping only weekends. If the other party also closes for federal holidays, add Christmas (Friday, December 25) and New Year's Day (Friday, January 1): the deadline moves to Thursday, January 14.

  • Within the 90-business-day window (April 6, 2027), add Martin Luther King Jr. Day (January 18) and Washington's Birthday (February 15), four holidays in all.
  • Within the 180-business-day window (August 10, 2027), add Memorial Day (May 31), Juneteenth observed on Friday, June 18 because the 19th is a Saturday, and Independence Day observed on Monday, July 5 because the 4th is a Sunday: seven holidays.

Banks and federal agencies follow this list; private companies choose their own. When a deadline lands on a weekend or holiday, many rules, including the federal tax deadline, roll it to the next business day; not every contract does.

Deadline questions people ask about counting days

What date is 90 days from today?
The box at the top always shows today’s answer for 30 days; type 90 in the number field and press Calculate.

Can I count backwards?
Yes. The result also lists the date the same number of days before your start date.

Is 30 days the same as 1 month?
Not exactly. Months have 28 to 31 days, so counting days gives a precise date.

Does today count?
No. Today is day 0, so tomorrow is day 1 and the result is day 30.

title: Hourly to Salary Calculator - Convert Hourly Wage to Annual Salary and Back
html:
Hourly to Salary Calculator

Convert
Amount
$
Hours per week
hours
Weeks worked per year (52 = paid vacation)
weeks

Before taxes and deductions. Overtime is not included.

Comparing job offers? Turn an hourly wage into a yearly salary — or a salary into an hourly rate — and see what each paycheck looks like.

Comparing hourly pay and salaries fairly

An hourly wage and a yearly salary only compare fairly when you use the same hours. This calculator turns either one into hourly, weekly, biweekly, semi-monthly, monthly and yearly figures.

How to use the hourly to salary calculator

  1. Choose hourly → salary or salary → hourly.
  2. Enter the amount, hours per week and weeks per year.
  3. Press Convert.

The formula

Yearly salary = hourly wage × hours per week × weeks per year

Worked examples

  • $25 an hour, 40 hours, 52 weeks = $52,000 a year — $4,333 a month, $2,000 every two weeks, or $2,167 twice a month.
  • A $85,000 salary at 40 hours × 52 weeks (2,080 hours) = $40.87 an hour.
  • If the same $25-an-hour job gives two unpaid weeks off, use 50 weeks: $50,000.

Case study: two offers, same job, very different hourly rates

Offer A is a $62,000 salary. The manager says a typical week is 45 hours. Offer B is $31 an hour, non-exempt, scheduled for 40 hours.

  • Offer A at 45 hours × 52 weeks = 2,340 hours, so $62,000 ÷ 2,340 = $26.50 an hour. Only at a true 40-hour week does it reach $29.81.
  • Offer B at 40 hours is $31 × 2,080 = $64,480 a year. If the job really runs 45 hours, the extra 5 are paid at time and a half ($46.50), making $1,472.50 a week or $76,570 a year.

Now add benefits. If Offer A includes employer health coverage worth $500 a month and Offer B has none, A is worth about $68,000 against B's $64,480 at 40 hours. The moment B's overtime becomes routine, B pulls ahead again. The decision rule: convert every offer to dollars per hour actually worked, then add benefits as a yearly dollar figure, never as a vague percentage.

Biweekly vs. semi-monthly

Pay schedulePaychecks a yearOn a $52,000 salary
Weekly52$1,000
Biweekly (every 2 weeks)26$2,000
Semi-monthly (twice a month)24$2,166.67
Monthly12$4,333.33

Biweekly pay means two months a year have three paychecks — handy for budgeting if you plan your bills on two checks a month.

What the numbers leave out

  • Overtime: under federal law, non-exempt workers earn 1.5 times their regular rate for hours over 40 in a week.
  • Benefits: health insurance, retirement matches and paid leave can be worth 20–30% on top of a salary.
  • Taxes: all figures are gross pay, before income tax, Social Security and Medicare.

Common mistakes

  • Using 4 weeks for a month: a month averages 4.33 weeks, so weekly pay × 4 understates monthly income.
  • Comparing a 37.5-hour job to a 40-hour job without changing the hours field.

Using it to compare job offers

When one offer is hourly and another is salaried, convert both to the same unit and include the expected hours. A salaried job that regularly needs 50 hours a week pays less per hour than the same salary at 40 hours.

Then add the value of benefits and commuting costs. A slightly lower salary with employer health insurance and a retirement match can be worth more than a higher hourly wage without them.

Salaried does not mean exempt from overtime

Federal law requires overtime at 1.5 times the regular rate for hours over 40 in a workweek for non-exempt employees. Being paid a salary is only one part of the exemption test; the job's actual duties must also qualify, and the salary must be above a federal threshold that has changed and been challenged in court in recent years. Check the Department of Labor's overtime page for the current figure rather than assuming a salary alone settles it.

States can go further. California, for example, requires daily overtime after 8 hours in a single day. Federal law has no daily rule and does not require extra pay for weekend or night work by itself.

For this calculator, a salaried worker with three weeks of paid vacation still enters 52 weeks, because the pay continues. An hourly worker who takes two unpaid weeks enters 50. At the $7.25 federal minimum, 40 hours for 52 weeks is $15,080 a year.

Wage and salary questions from job seekers

What is the federal minimum wage?
$7.25 an hour, but many states and cities set higher minimums. Check your state labor department.

How much is $20 an hour a year?
About $41,600 at 40 hours a week for 52 weeks.

What is the difference between biweekly and semi-monthly?
Biweekly is every two weeks (26 checks); semi-monthly is twice a month (24 checks).
