title: Mortgage Calculator - Monthly Payment with Taxes, Insurance and PMI
html:
Mortgage Calculator

Home price
$
Down payment
%
Interest rate
% per year
Loan term
Property tax (US average is about 1%)
% per year
Home insurance
$per year
HOA fees (optional)
$per month

PMI is estimated at 0.5% of the loan per year when the down payment is under 20%. Estimates only — ask your lender for an official quote.

Buying a home is the biggest purchase most people ever make. This free mortgage calculator shows your full monthly payment — not just principal and interest, but also property tax, homeowners insurance, PMI and HOA fees — so you know what you can really afford.

A practical guide to your mortgage payment

The number most lenders quote first is principal and interest. The number that actually leaves your bank account every month is larger, because it usually also includes property tax, homeowners insurance, private mortgage insurance (PMI) and, in some neighborhoods, HOA dues. People are often surprised that taxes and insurance can add 25–40% on top of the loan payment itself. This calculator shows the full monthly figure so you can compare it with your budget honestly, not with the advertised rate.

How to use the mortgage calculator

  1. Enter the home price and your down payment as a percent.
  2. Enter the interest rate your lender quoted and pick the loan term.
  3. Adjust property tax, insurance and HOA if you know them.
  4. Press Calculate Payment to see the monthly total and the full breakdown.

The formula

Monthly P&I = L × r ÷ (1 − (1 + r)−n)
L = loan amount, r = monthly rate (annual rate ÷ 12), n = number of monthly payments

What goes into the monthly payment (PITI)

  • Principal – the part that pays down what you borrowed. Early in the loan it is small; it grows every month.
  • Interest – the lender's charge. On a 30-year loan, the first years are mostly interest.
  • Taxes – your county's property tax, usually collected monthly into an escrow account and paid once or twice a year by the lender.
  • Insurance – homeowners insurance (required by the lender), also usually paid through escrow.
  • PMI – required on most conventional loans when the down payment is under 20%. It typically costs about 0.3%–1.5% of the loan per year and can be removed once you reach 20% equity.

Paying one point to cut the rate: a $320,000 break-even

A discount point costs 1% of the loan amount and buys a lower rate. Lenders price points differently, but a common quote is roughly 0.25 percentage points off the rate per point. Here is what that trade looks like on a $320,000, 30-year loan.

  • No points, 6.5%: principal and interest of about $2,023 a month.
  • One point ($3,200) for 6.25%: about $1,970 a month.
  • Monthly saving: about $52 (the unrounded payments are $2,022.62 and $1,970.30). Break-even: $3,200 ÷ $52 ≈ 61 months, or about five years.

The decision rule is simple: if you expect to keep this loan longer than the break-even, the point pays for itself; if you might sell or refinance sooner, skip it. On the official Loan Estimate, points appear in Section A of the closing costs, and the APR already includes them, which is why APR, not the rate, is the fair basis for comparing two offers.

Worked example: a $400,000 home

Suppose the price is $400,000, you put down 10% ($40,000) and borrow $360,000 at 6.5% for 30 years. The principal-and-interest payment is about $2,275. Add property tax of 1.1% a year ($367/month), insurance of $1,800 a year ($150/month) and PMI of 0.6% of the loan ($180/month). The real payment is roughly $2,972 a month — almost $700 more than the "headline" figure.

Now change one thing: put down 20% instead. The loan falls to $320,000, principal and interest drop to about $2,023, and PMI disappears. The total is about $2,540 — around $430 a month less. That is why the down payment field matters so much.

15-year vs 30-year: the real trade-off

$320,000 loanRateMonthly P&ITotal interest
30-year6.5%≈ $2,023≈ $408,000
15-year5.9%≈ $2,683≈ $163,000

The 15-year loan costs about $660 more each month but saves roughly $245,000 in interest. A common middle path is to take the 30-year loan for flexibility and make extra principal payments when you can — even $200 extra a month can shorten a 30-year loan by several years.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Using the rate instead of the APR to compare lenders. The APR includes points and fees; compare loans using the same APR basis on the official Loan Estimate.
  • Leaving out taxes and insurance. They vary widely by state and county. Check the listing or the county assessor's site for the actual tax.
  • Forgetting PMI ends. On conventional loans you can ask to cancel PMI at 20% equity, and it usually ends automatically at 22%.
  • Budgeting to the maximum approval. Lenders approve based on debt ratios, not on your savings goals, childcare or repairs. Many planners suggest keeping total housing costs near 28% of gross income.

What an extra $200 a month does to a 30-year loan

The same $320,000 loan at 6.5% requires $2,023 a month. Suppose you pay $2,223 instead and ask the servicer to apply the extra $200 to principal.

Monthly paymentMonths to pay offTotal interest
$2,023 (required)360about $408,000
$2,223 (+$200 extra)about 280about $303,000
$2,683 (15-year loan at 5.9%)180about $163,000

The extra $200 ends the loan roughly 6 years 8 months early and saves about $105,000 in interest, with no new contract and no closing costs. You keep the right to stop the extra payment in a tight month, which the 15-year loan does not allow. Before you start, confirm with the servicer that extra money is applied to principal, not held for next month's payment, and check your closing disclosure for a prepayment penalty; most conventional loans have none.

Mortgage questions readers send us

Why did my escrow payment change?
Your lender reviews escrow once a year. If property tax or insurance went up, your monthly payment rises even though your rate is fixed.

Does a bigger down payment always make sense?
It lowers the payment and can remove PMI, but keep an emergency fund of several months of expenses. Being "house rich, cash poor" is risky if repairs or job changes come up.

How accurate is this calculator?
It uses the standard amortization formula lenders use for fixed-rate loans. Your official Loan Estimate will differ slightly because of exact tax and insurance quotes, points and rounding.

What about adjustable-rate (ARM) loans?
This calculator assumes a fixed rate. For an ARM, run it once at the starting rate and again at the maximum rate allowed after adjustment to see the worst case.

What is PITI?
PITI stands for Principal, Interest, Taxes and Insurance — the four parts of a typical monthly mortgage payment.

When does PMI go away?
On conventional loans, PMI can usually be removed once you reach 20% equity, and it ends automatically at 22% equity based on the original schedule.

Is the rate the same as APR?
No. APR includes some fees and closing costs, so it is usually a little higher than the interest rate used here.

title: Percentage Calculator - What Is X% of Y, Percent Change and Percent Of
html:
Percentage Calculator

What do you want to find?
X
Y

Results are rounded to two decimal places.

Discounts, tips, raises, test scores, stock moves — percentages are everywhere. Pick the question you have, enter two numbers, and get the answer instantly.

Three percentage questions, explained simply

Almost every percentage problem is one of three questions. Knowing which one you are asking makes the math easy.

QuestionFormulaExample
What is X% of Y?Y × X ÷ 10015% of 80 = 12
X is what % of Y?X ÷ Y × 10012 is 15% of 80
% change from A to B(B − A) ÷ A × 10080 → 92 = +15%

How to use the percentage calculator

  1. Choose the type of question.
  2. Enter X and Y.
  3. Press Calculate.

The formula

X% of Y = Y × X ÷ 100  |  Percent change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100

Everyday examples

  • Sales: a $120 jacket at 25% off saves $30, so you pay $90.
  • Raises: going from $52,000 to $54,600 is a 5% raise.
  • Tips: 18% of a $64 bill is $11.52.
  • Price increases: a bill that rose from $150 to $165 went up 10%.

Discount today, markup needed to get back to the original price

A percentage cut and the percentage rise that undoes it are never the same number, because the second one is measured from a smaller base. The gain needed to recover from a loss of d is d ÷ (1 − d).

Value falls byGain needed to get back
10%11.1%
20%25%
25%33.3%
40%66.7%
50%100%
75%300%

Example: a stock bought at $80 drops 40% to $48. Getting back to $80 means rising $32 on a $48 base, which is 66.7%, not 40%. The same logic explains why a portfolio that loses 50% and then gains 50% ends at 75% of where it started: $100 → $50 → $75. For a shopper, a store that marks a jacket down 25% and later raises the sale price by 25% is still selling it below the original tag: $120 → $90 → $112.50.

Mistakes that trip people up

Up and down are not symmetrical. If a price rises 20% and then falls 20%, you don't return to the start: $100 → $120 → $96. Percent vs percentage points: a rate moving from 4% to 5% is a 1 percentage point increase, but a 25% relative increase. Stacked discounts multiply: 30% off and then another 10% off is 37% off in total, not 40%.

Mental-math shortcuts

  • 10% → move the decimal one place (10% of $84 = $8.40).
  • 5% → half of 10%. 20% → double 10%.
  • X% of Y equals Y% of X — 8% of 50 is the same as 50% of 8 = 4.

Yearly percent changes compound; they do not simply add

When a change repeats, multiply the growth factors instead of adding the percentages.

  • Rent rising 5% a year for six years: 1.05 raised to the sixth power is 1.34, a 34% total increase, not 30%. A $1,500 rent becomes about $2,010.
  • Inflation of 3%, 4% and 3% over three years: 1.03 × 1.04 × 1.03 = 1.103, so prices are up 10.3%, not 10%.
  • An investment up 50% over five years grew about 8.45% a year, not 10%, because 1.0845 compounded for five years is about 1.50. The Investor.gov compound interest calculator lets you check this kind of figure.
  • To undo a 25% increase, divide by 1.25 rather than subtracting 25%: $125 ÷ 1.25 = $100, while $125 × 0.75 = $93.75.

The percent change option above handles one step at a time. For a multi-year question, run each step on the previous result, or multiply the factors as shown and subtract 1 at the end.

Percentage puzzles readers ask about

How do I find the original price before a discount?
Divide the sale price by (1 − discount). $90 after 25% off: 90 ÷ 0.75 = $120.

How do I add sales tax?
Multiply by (1 + rate). $50 with 8% tax: 50 × 1.08 = $54.

How do I calculate a discount?
Use “What is X% of Y?” to get the discount amount, then subtract it from the price.

How do I reverse a percentage?
If a price after a 20% discount is $80, the original is 80 ÷ (1 − 0.20) = $100.

Related calculators

Tip Calculator · Inflation Calculator · Grade Calculator

Sources and further reading

  • Investor.gov (SEC) – Compound Interest Calculator

BMI Calculator

For adults 20 and older. BMI does not measure body fat directly; talk to a doctor about your health.

Body Mass Index (BMI) is a quick screening number that compares your weight with your height. Enter your measurements in feet and pounds or centimeters and kilograms to see your BMI and healthy weight range.

What your BMI does — and doesn't — tell you

Body mass index compares weight with height. It is a quick screening number doctors use to spot possible weight-related health risks across large groups of people. It does not measure body fat directly, so it should be read alongside other information such as waist size, blood pressure and blood tests.

How to use the bmi calculator

  1. Choose US or metric units.
  2. Enter your height and weight.
  3. Press Calculate BMI.

The formula

BMI = 703 × weight (lb) ÷ height (in)²  =  weight (kg) ÷ height (m)²

Worked example

Height 5 ft 9 in (69 inches), weight 170 lb. BMI = 703 × 170 ÷ 69² = 25.1, just inside the "overweight" range. In metric: 77 kg ÷ (1.75 m)² ≈ 25.1.

BMI (adults)Category
Below 18.5Underweight
18.5–24.9Healthy weight
25.0–29.9Overweight
30 and aboveObesity

Pounds per BMI point, by height

Because BMI divides weight by height squared, one BMI point is a different number of pounds depending on how tall you are. The conversion is height in inches squared ÷ 703.

HeightPounds per BMI pointWeight change from 27.0 to 24.9 (2.1 points)
5 ft 0 in5.1 lb10.8 lb
5 ft 4 in5.8 lb12.2 lb
5 ft 8 in6.6 lb13.8 lb
6 ft 0 in7.4 lb15.5 lb
6 ft 4 in8.2 lb17.3 lb

Worked case: someone 5 ft 4 in and 160 lb has a BMI of 703 × 160 ÷ 4,096 = 27.5. Reaching 24.9 means dropping about 2.6 points × 5.8 lb, roughly 15 lb, to about 145 lb. In metric, one BMI point equals your height in meters squared, in kilograms: at 1.70 m, 2.89 kg.

Limits of BMI

  • Muscle – athletes can have a high BMI with little body fat.
  • Age – older adults may have more body fat at the same BMI.
  • Ethnicity – some health bodies use lower cut-offs for people of Asian descent.
  • Children and teens – BMI is interpreted with age- and sex-specific percentile charts, not the adult table.
  • Pregnancy – BMI is not used during pregnancy.

A useful companion: waist size

Fat around the abdomen is linked to higher risk. Many guidelines treat a waist over about 40 inches (102 cm) for men or 35 inches (88 cm) for women as a sign to talk with a doctor, even when BMI looks normal.

Worth knowing

  • Muscular people may have a high BMI without extra fat.

Three cases where the standard cut-offs can mislead

  1. Asian ancestry. A World Health Organization expert group suggested lower action points for Asian populations, 23 for overweight and 27.5 for obesity, because health risks appear at lower BMIs. The American Diabetes Association recommends diabetes screening for Asian Americans from a BMI of 23 rather than 25.
  2. Height that has changed. Many adults lose height with age but keep the number from an old driver's license. At 170 lb, a height of 69 in gives a BMI of 25.1; the same weight at 68 in gives 25.8. Measure yourself before you enter the number.
  3. Muscle and frame. Someone who lifts weights can read 27 with a 32-inch waist and low body fat. In that case the waist measurement and a blood pressure and cholesterol check say more than the table. The NIH describes BMI as a screening step, not a measure of body fat.

None of these changes the calculation, only what the number means; if one applies to you, treat the result as a prompt to talk with a clinician.

What people want to know about BMI

How much should I lose to change category?
Use the healthy-weight table on this page for your height; small changes of 5–10% of body weight already improve many health markers.

Is BMI a diagnosis?
No. It's a screening tool. Talk with a health professional about your own situation.

Is BMI accurate?
It is a useful screening tool for groups, but it does not separate muscle from fat. Use it alongside waist size and a doctor’s advice.

What BMI is considered obese?
For adults, a BMI of 30 or higher is classified as obesity by the CDC and WHO.

Related calculators

Calorie Calculator

Sources and further reading

  • CDC – About Body Mass Index (adult categories and limits)
  • NIH NHLBI – BMI calculator and healthy weight guidance

How we checked this page: formula and categories follow the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention adult BMI guidance (cdc.gov). This page is not medical advice. Last reviewed November 2026. BMI is a screening estimate, not a diagnosis or medical advice; discuss your results with a healthcare professional.

title: Due Date Calculator - When Is My Baby Due? Weeks Pregnant and Trimester
html:
Pregnancy Due Date Calculator

First day of your last period (LMP)
Average cycle length
days

Uses Naegele’s rule adjusted for cycle length. Only about 4% of babies are born on their due date — your doctor or midwife will confirm with an ultrasound.

Congratulations! Find your estimated due date, how far along you are today and when each trimester begins. All you need is the first day of your last menstrual period.

How your due date is estimated

Pregnancy is counted from the first day of your last menstrual period (LMP), not from conception, which for a typical 28-day cycle happens about two weeks later. A full-term pregnancy is estimated at 280 days, or 40 weeks, from the LMP. This is known as Naegele's rule, and it's the same starting point most clinics use before an ultrasound.

How to use the due date calculator

  1. Choose the first day of your last period.
  2. Enter your usual cycle length (28 days is typical).
  3. Press Calculate Due Date.

The formula

Due date = first day of last period + 280 days (+ cycle length − 28)

Worked example

If your last period started on January 1, 2026, adding 280 days gives an estimated due date of October 8, 2026. If your cycle is usually 32 days rather than 28, ovulation tends to happen later, so the estimate moves about 4 days later.

Worked calendar: a last period starting March 1, 2026

Counting 280 days forward from March 1, 2026 gives a due date of December 6, 2026. Every milestone follows from the same count, 7 days per week.

MilestoneDays from LMPDate
12 weeks 0 days84May 24, 2026
20 weeks 0 days (anatomy scan window)140July 19, 2026
28 weeks 0 days (third trimester)196September 13, 2026
37 weeks 0 days (early term)259November 15, 2026
39 weeks 0 days (full term)273November 29, 2026
40 weeks 0 days (due date)280December 6, 2026

Post-term begins at 42 weeks, December 20. To find how far along you are on any day, count days from the LMP and divide by 7: June 15, 2026 is day 106, or 15 weeks 1 day. With a 32-day cycle, ovulation comes about 4 days later, so the due date and every milestone shift 4 days later (December 10).

Why the date is only an estimate

Only about 1 in 20 babies arrive on the exact due date. Most are born between 37 and 42 weeks. An early ultrasound, especially in the first trimester, is the most accurate way to date a pregnancy, and your provider may adjust the due date based on it. If you conceived through IVF, the transfer date gives a very precise estimate.

Trimesters at a glance

TrimesterWeeksTypical milestones
First1–13First prenatal visit, dating ultrasound, early screening options
Second14–27Anatomy scan around 18–22 weeks; glucose test around 24–28 weeks
Third28–40+More frequent visits; group B strep test around 36–37 weeks

Term definitions

  • Early term: 37 weeks 0 days to 38 weeks 6 days
  • Full term: 39 weeks 0 days to 40 weeks 6 days
  • Late term: 41 weeks 0 days to 41 weeks 6 days
  • Post-term: 42 weeks and beyond

Before you rely on the number

  • Start a prenatal vitamin with folic acid as early as possible.

When an ultrasound replaces the period-based date

Under American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists guidance, the LMP date stands unless an ultrasound differs from it by more than a set number of days, and the allowance grows as pregnancy advances.

Ultrasound performed atRedate if the difference is more than
Up to 8 weeks 6 days5 days
9 weeks 0 days to 15 weeks 6 days7 days
16 weeks 0 days to 21 weeks 6 days10 days
22 weeks 0 days to 27 weeks 6 days14 days
28 weeks 0 days and later21 days

Example: your LMP puts you at 8 weeks 2 days, and the scan measures 7 weeks 4 days. The gap is 5 days, so the LMP date stays. Had the scan read 7 weeks 3 days, the 6-day gap would move your due date 6 days later. Once set this way, the date is normally not changed again, even if a later scan suggests a bigger or smaller baby; IVF pregnancies are dated from the transfer instead.

Questions expectant parents ask most

I don't remember my last period. What now?
An ultrasound can date the pregnancy. Contact your healthcare provider.

Can I use this if my cycles are irregular?
It gives a rough estimate, but an ultrasound will be more reliable.

How accurate is a due date?
It is an estimate. An early ultrasound is the most accurate way to date a pregnancy.

Why count from my last period instead of conception?
Conception date is rarely known exactly, so doctors count from the last period, which adds about 2 weeks.

Related calculators

Date Calculator · Age Calculator

Sources and further reading

  • ACOG – Women's health FAQs (pregnancy dating, term definitions)
  • U.S. Naval Observatory – Astronomical Applications (calendar and date tools)

Before you fall in love with a house, find out what price fits your budget. This calculator uses the same debt-to-income rules many lenders use to estimate how much house you can afford.

How much house is comfortable, not just possible

Lenders mostly look at two ratios. The front-end ratio is your total housing payment (principal, interest, taxes, insurance, PMI, HOA) divided by gross monthly income; many lenders like it at or below about 28%. The back-end ratio adds all other monthly debt payments — car, student loans, minimum card payments — and is often capped around 36% to 43%. This calculator uses both and reports the lower result, so you see a price that passes both tests.

How to use the home affordability calculator

  1. Enter your yearly income before taxes and your monthly debt payments.
  2. Enter the down payment you have saved and a mortgage rate.
  3. Pick a comfortable or stretch budget.
  4. Press Calculate.

The formula

Housing cost ≤ 28% of gross monthly income, and housing + other debts ≤ 36%

IncomeMax housing / month (28%)Approx. price*
$60,000$1,400$222,000
$100,000$2,333$370,000
$150,000$3,500$555,000

Worked example: $90,000 income

Gross monthly income is $7,500. At 28%, the housing budget is about $2,100. If taxes and insurance run about $500 a month, $1,600 is left for principal and interest. At 6.5% for 30 years, that supports a loan of roughly $253,000. With 10% down, that points to a home price around $280,000. If you also have a $450 car payment, the back-end limit may lower that number further.

Property tax and HOA dues quietly shrink the price you can afford

Two $350,000 houses can carry very different monthly costs, and lenders count every dollar of tax and dues against the same 28% ceiling.

  • At a 0.6% property tax rate, tax is $350,000 × 0.006 ÷ 12 = $175 a month.
  • At 2.0%, it is $583 a month, a difference of $408.
  • At 6.5% over 30 years, each $1,000 borrowed costs about $6.32 a month, so $408 a month supports about $64,500 of loan.

In other words, the buyer in the high-tax county qualifies for roughly $64,000 less house on the same income. A $300 monthly HOA fee works the same way and trims about $47,500 from the loan. Before you compare listings, pull the actual tax bill from the county assessor's site and the HOA budget from the seller's disclosures, then use the real tax rate here rather than a national average; the calculator has no HOA field, so subtract any dues from your monthly housing budget by hand.

What changes the result the most

  • Interest rate – each 1 percentage point higher reduces the affordable loan by roughly 10%.
  • Other debts – paying off a car loan before buying can raise your budget more than a raise would.
  • Property tax – two homes at the same price can have very different monthly costs in different counties.
  • Down payment – 20% removes PMI on most conventional loans.

Leave room for real life

The ratios don't know about childcare, retirement saving or the roof that will need replacing. A common budgeting rule is to set aside 1–2% of the home's value each year for maintenance, and to keep an emergency fund after closing. Many buyers choose a price below their approval to keep that cushion.

Six checks before you set a price ceiling

  1. Run both ratios and keep the lower result. A $450 car payment can cap you under the 36% back-end test even when the 28% housing test passes.
  2. Count closing costs and reserves against your savings. With $60,000 saved, 3% closing costs on a $350,000 home ($10,500) and $9,000 of reserves leave $40,500 for the down payment, about 11.6%, so PMI applies.
  3. Test the payment against take-home pay. A $2,100 housing payment is 28% of $7,500 gross but about 37% of a $5,700 paycheck.
  4. Stress-test the rate. Rerun the numbers 1 percentage point higher; if the result no longer fits, you are relying on a rate lock holding.
  5. Budget maintenance. At 1–2% of value a year, a $350,000 home needs $290–$580 a month set aside.
  6. Check the loan program's own limits. FHA and other programs use their own ratio caps and insurance costs, so a lender's quote can differ from the 28/36 estimate here.

Affordability questions buyers raise

Gross or take-home pay?
Lenders use gross (before tax). For your own budget, check the payment against take-home pay too.

Do closing costs matter?
Yes — they are often 2–5% of the price and are paid in cash on top of the down payment.

Does my credit score change affordability?
Indirectly: a better score gets a lower rate, which raises the loan you can afford at the same payment.

What is the 28/36 rule?
Housing costs should be no more than 28% of gross income, and all debt payments no more than 36%.

*How was the table estimated?
It assumes no other debt, 20% down, a 6.5% 30-year loan and 1.5% yearly tax and insurance.

html:
Calorie Calculator (TDEE)

Sex

Uses the Mifflin-St Jeor equation. Do not go below about 1,200 (women) or 1,500 (men) calories a day without medical advice.

How many calories do you burn in a day? This calculator estimates your Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) and Total Daily Energy Expenditure (TDEE), then shows calorie targets for losing or gaining weight.

Understanding BMR, TDEE and your daily calories

BMR (basal metabolic rate) is the energy your body uses at complete rest — breathing, circulation, keeping warm. TDEE (total daily energy expenditure) adds everything you do: walking, work, exercise. This calculator estimates BMR with the Mifflin–St Jeor equation, which studies have found to be one of the more accurate formulas for most adults, then multiplies it by an activity factor.

How to use the calorie calculator

  1. Choose your sex and enter your age.
  2. Enter your height and weight in US or metric units.
  3. Pick your activity level.
  4. Press Calculate Calories.

The formula

Mifflin-St Jeor BMR = 10 × kg + 6.25 × cm − 5 × age + 5 (men) or − 161 (women)  |  TDEE = BMR × activity

Worked example

A 40-year-old man, 178 cm (5 ft 10 in), 80 kg (176 lb): BMR = 10 × 80 + 6.25 × 178 − 5 × 40 + 5 ≈ 1,718 kcal. With moderate exercise 3–5 days a week (×1.55), TDEE ≈ 2,660 kcal a day.

Activity levelMultiplier
Mostly sitting1.2
Light exercise 1–3 days1.375
Moderate 3–5 days1.55
Hard 6–7 days1.725

Myth versus fact: calorie claims that do not survive the math

  • Myth: a 500-calorie daily deficit always loses 52 pounds a year. Fact: in the Mifflin-St Jeor equation every kilogram lost lowers BMR by about 10 calories a day, so the same menu buys a smaller deficit as weight falls and loss slows.
  • Myth: food eaten after 8 p.m. turns to fat. Fact: the daily balance of calories in and out drives weight; timing matters mostly through sleep and appetite.
  • Myth: a pound of muscle burns 50 calories a day. Fact: resting muscle uses roughly 6 calories per pound per day, about three times fat tissue.
  • Myth: 2,000 calories is the right number for everyone. Fact: 2,000 is the reference used for percent Daily Values on Nutrition Facts labels. The Dietary Guidelines for Americans estimate adult needs at roughly 1,600–2,400 calories for women and 2,000–3,000 for men, depending on age and activity.
  • Myth: drinks are a rounding error. Fact: alcohol has about 7 calories per gram, so a 5-ounce glass of wine is around 120 calories, and a cocktail adds the mixer on top.

Using the number for a goal

  • Maintain: eat close to your TDEE.
  • Lose weight gradually: a deficit of about 300–500 kcal a day is a common, sustainable starting point.
  • Gain muscle: a small surplus (about 200–300 kcal) with strength training.

Most people overestimate their activity level. If your weight doesn't change as expected after 2–3 weeks, adjust by 100–200 kcal rather than making big cuts.

Safety notes

Very low intakes are hard to sustain and can cause nutrient shortfalls. People who are pregnant or breastfeeding, under 18, or managing a medical condition should get personal advice from a doctor or registered dietitian.

Small details that change the result

  • Protein and fiber help you feel full on fewer calories.

Worked case: why the same menu stops working after 15 pounds

A 35-year-old woman, 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) and 75 kg (165 lb), with light activity (multiplier 1.375):

  • BMR = 10 × 75 + 6.25 × 165 − 5 × 35 − 161 = 1,445 calories.
  • TDEE = 1,445 × 1.375 ≈ 1,987 calories. A 400-calorie deficit means eating about 1,590.
  • After losing 7 kg (about 15 lb) to 68 kg: BMR = 1,375 and TDEE ≈ 1,891.
  • Still eating 1,590, the deficit is now about 300 calories, roughly a quarter smaller, so weekly loss slows in step.

The fix is to recalculate at each 10-pound milestone and either trim 100 calories or add activity, not to cut sharply, while staying above the usual floors of about 1,200 calories for women and 1,500 for men without medical supervision. USDA FoodData Central gives actual calorie counts for the foods you log, which beats guessing from a package label.

Calorie counting questions, answered

Why is my BMR lower than I expected?
BMR drops with age and with lower muscle mass. Strength training helps maintain it.

Do I eat back exercise calories?
If you chose an activity level that already includes exercise, no — it's counted in your TDEE.

What is the difference between BMR and TDEE?
BMR is what your body burns at complete rest. TDEE adds daily movement and exercise.

Is the Mifflin-St Jeor equation accurate?
It is considered one of the most accurate simple formulas, usually within about 10% for most people.

Related calculators

BMI Calculator

Sources and further reading

  • Dietary Guidelines for Americans – estimated calorie needs by age, sex and activity
  • USDA FoodData Central – nutrient and calorie database

title: GPA Calculator - Calculate Your Semester and Cumulative GPA (4.0 Scale)
html:
GPA Calculator

Courses this term
CourseGradeCredits
Previous cumulative GPA (leave blank if first term)
Previous total credits

Uses the common 4.0 scale (A = 4.0, A- = 3.7 … F = 0). Some schools use different values.

Find out your grade point average in seconds. Enter each class’s letter grade and credit hours to get your term GPA, and add your previous GPA to see your updated cumulative GPA.

How GPA is calculated

Your GPA is a credit-weighted average. Each letter grade is turned into grade points (A = 4.0, B = 3.0 and so on), multiplied by the course's credit hours, and the total is divided by the total credits. A 4-credit class therefore moves your GPA more than a 1-credit class.

How to use the gpa calculator

  1. For each course, pick the letter grade and enter the credit hours.
  2. Optionally enter your previous cumulative GPA and credits.
  3. Press Calculate GPA.

The formula

GPA = Σ (grade points × credits) ÷ Σ credits

Worked example

CourseCreditsGradePoints
Biology4B (3.0)12.0
English3A (4.0)12.0
History3B+ (3.3)9.9
Statistics2C (2.0)4.0

Total points 37.9 ÷ 12 credits = 3.16 GPA.

Worked case: from 3.2 at 60 credits to a 3.5 at graduation

Grade points, not GPAs, are what add up. A 3.2 over 60 credits is 192 grade points. A 3.5 over 120 credits requires 420. The remaining 60 credits must therefore supply 228 points, an average of 3.80.

Target cumulative GPA at 120 creditsPoints still neededAverage required over the last 60 credits
3.32043.40
3.42163.60
3.52283.80
3.62404.00

A 3.80 average is roughly two A's for every A- or B+, every term, so a 3.5 is possible but leaves no slack; a 3.4 is a more realistic plan. One shortcut exists at some schools: grade replacement. Retaking a 4-credit course graded D (1.0) and earning a B (3.0) adds 8 points to the 60 credits already on the record, lifting 192 ÷ 60 = 3.20 to 200 ÷ 60 = 3.33 in a single term. Check your catalog, since other schools average both attempts or cap how many courses can be replaced.

Cumulative GPA

To combine semesters, don't average the GPAs — weight them by credits. If you had a 3.4 over 30 credits and earn a 3.0 over 15 credits, your cumulative GPA is (3.4 × 30 + 3.0 × 15) ÷ 45 = 3.27.

How much can one semester raise your GPA?

The more credits you've completed, the harder it is to move. After 90 credits at 2.8, a perfect 4.0 over 15 credits only raises you to about 2.97. Planning early matters; so does knowing your school's retake policy, since some schools replace the old grade.

Weighted vs unweighted (high school)

Many high schools add a point for honors, AP or IB courses (an A counts as 5.0). Colleges often recalculate GPA their own way, so report what your school's transcript shows.

Where a GPA threshold actually bites: federal aid, scholarships, applications

  • Federal student aid. Schools must check satisfactory academic progress. Under federal rules, by the end of the second academic year a student must have at least a C average (2.0 on this scale) or standing consistent with graduating, and must be completing courses fast enough to finish within 150% of the program length. Falling short can suspend Pell Grants and federal loans until an appeal succeeds or grades recover.
  • Merit scholarships. Renewal minimums are commonly set at 3.0 on the cumulative GPA, so one weak 15-credit term after a 3.1 start can cost the award.
  • Transcripts and applications. Point values differ by school: some give an A+ 4.3, others 4.0; an A- may be 3.67 or 3.7. Graduate and professional programs often recalculate on their own scale, sometimes on the last 60 credits only, so report what your transcript shows and let them convert.

GPA questions from students and parents

Do pass/fail courses count?
Usually not in the GPA, though they count toward credits.

What is a good GPA?
It depends on the goal: many scholarships and graduate programs look for 3.0–3.5 or higher.

What is the difference between weighted and unweighted GPA?
Unweighted GPA uses the 4.0 scale above. Weighted GPA adds extra points for honors or AP classes, up to about 5.0.

Related calculators

Grade Calculator · Percentage Calculator

Sources and further reading

  • Federal Student Aid – satisfactory academic progress and keeping your aid
  • Khan Academy – Arithmetic: weighted averages and decimals

How we checked this page: examples checked by hand using the common 4.0 scale; schools may use slightly different point values for plus/minus grades. Last reviewed November 2026. GPA results are estimates on a common scale; your registrar's official transcript and your school's policies take precedence.

If the end time is earlier than the start time, it is treated as the next day (overnight shift).

Need to fill in a time card, check a paycheck or plan a schedule? This calculator counts hours between two times — including unpaid breaks and overnight shifts — and converts them to decimal hours and pay.

Calculating work hours without mistakes

Adding up time is harder than adding normal numbers because an hour has 60 minutes, not 100. That's where most timesheet errors come from. This calculator handles minutes, overnight shifts and unpaid breaks, and shows the result both as hours and minutes and as a decimal for payroll.

How to use the hours calculator

  1. Choose “Hours between two times” or “Add or subtract time”.
  2. Pick the times with hours, minutes and AM/PM.
  3. Enter a break or an hourly rate if you like.
  4. Press Calculate.

The formula

Hours worked = end time − start time − break  |  decimal hours = minutes ÷ 60

Worked example

Clock in 8:45 AM, clock out 5:15 PM, with a 30-minute unpaid lunch. 8:45 to 5:15 is 8 hours 30 minutes; minus 30 minutes gives 8 hours, or 8.00 decimal hours. At $22 an hour that day is $176.

Worked week: five punches, one overtime check

DayInOutUnpaid breakHoursDecimal
Mon8:00 AM4:40 PM30 min8 h 10 m8.17
Tue7:55 AM5:05 PM30 min8 h 40 m8.67
Wed8:00 AM4:30 PM30 min8 h 00 m8.00
Thu8:00 AM6:15 PM30 min9 h 45 m9.75
Fri8:00 AM4:00 PM30 min7 h 30 m7.50
Week42 h 05 m42.08

Under the Fair Labor Standards Act, overtime is owed for hours over 40 in a single workweek. At $20 an hour: 40 × $20 = $800, plus 2.08 overtime hours × $30 = $62.50, for $862.50. The workweek counts, not the pay period: 45 hours one week and 35 the next is 5 overtime hours even though the two-week total is 80. And decimals come from minutes ÷ 60, so 42 hours 5 minutes is 42.08, not 42.05.

Minutes to decimal hours

MinutesDecimalMinutesDecimal
60.10300.50
150.25450.75
200.33500.83

A common error is writing 7 hours 30 minutes as "7.30". In decimal it is 7.5 — writing 7.30 underpays by 12 minutes.

Overnight shifts

If you start at 10:00 PM and finish at 6:30 AM, the end time is "earlier" than the start time. The calculator treats it as the next day: the shift is 8 hours 30 minutes.

Overtime basics (U.S.)

Under the federal Fair Labor Standards Act, most non-exempt employees earn at least 1.5 times their regular rate for hours over 40 in a workweek. Some states, such as California, also have daily overtime rules. Total your weekly hours here, then check your state's rules.

Before you rely on the number

  • Night shifts that pass midnight are handled automatically.

Rounding, daily overtime and a 2026 tax wrinkle

  • Rounding is legal within limits. Federal regulations allow rounding punches to the nearest 5 minutes, tenth of an hour or quarter hour, provided the practice does not consistently favor the employer. Under quarter-hour rounding, 8:07 becomes 8:00 but 8:08 becomes 8:15.
  • Some states count the day, not just the week. California requires 1.5× pay after 8 hours in a day and 2× after 12, so the Thursday shift above would carry 1 hour 45 minutes of overtime even in a short week. Alaska, Nevada and Colorado have their own daily rules with different triggers.
  • The overtime premium is deductible for 2025 through 2028. A 2025 federal law lets workers deduct the premium half of FLSA overtime, the extra $10 an hour in the example above ($20.83 for the week), up to $12,500 a year for a single filer or $25,000 on a joint return, with phase-outs at higher incomes.

Apply your state's daily rule on top of the 40-hour test and use whichever gives more pay.

Timesheet and overtime questions

Are breaks paid?
Under federal rules, short breaks (about 5–20 minutes) are usually paid; meal breaks of 30 minutes or more where you are fully relieved of duty usually are not.

How do I add up a whole week?
Calculate each day, convert to decimal hours, then add the decimals.

How do I convert minutes to decimal hours?
Divide the minutes by 60. For example 40 minutes ÷ 60 = 0.67 hours.

Does the break count as work time?
Short breaks (usually under 20 minutes) are generally paid; meal breaks of 30 minutes or more are often unpaid. Check your state rules.

Related calculators

  • U.S. Department of Labor – Overtime pay under the FLSA

  • IRS – federal tax information, including the overtime deduction

title: Dice Roller - Roll Virtual Dice Online (d6, d20, d100 and More)
html:
Dice Roller

Number of dice
Sides per die
Modifier (add or subtract, e.g. 3 or -2)

Uses your browser’s secure random number generator — every roll is fair.

Lost the dice for game night? Roll up to ten virtual dice — classic six-sided or the d4, d8, d10, d12, d20 and d100 used in tabletop role-playing games.

Dice odds made simple

Every die roll here is independent and uses your browser’s cryptographic random number generator, so no number is favored. Knowing the odds helps with board games and tabletop RPGs.

How to use the dice roller

  1. Choose how many dice and how many sides.
  2. Add a modifier if your game uses one.
  3. Press Roll the Dice as many times as you like.

The formula

Each die is an independent random whole number from 1 to the number of sides

Two six-sided dice (2d6)

TotalWaysChance
2 or 1212.8%
3 or 1125.6%
4 or 1038.3%
5 or 9411.1%
6 or 8513.9%
7616.7%

There are 36 equally likely outcomes. Seven is the most common total because six combinations make it (1+6, 2+5, 3+4 and the reverses).

Odds of rolling at least one six

Many games only need a six (or a natural 20) on at least one die. The quickest way to find that chance is backwards: work out the odds that every die misses, then subtract from 100%. One die misses a six 5 times in 6, so with several dice you multiply 5/6 by itself once per die.

Dice rolledChance of at least one 6
116.7%
230.6%
342.1%
451.8%
666.5%

Four dice is the first point where a six is more likely than not, and you need 13 dice to pass 90%. The same method works for a d20: swap 5/6 for 19/20, and two d20s show at least one natural 20 only 9.75% of the time.

d20 rolls

  • Each face of a d20 has a 5% chance, so a natural 20 comes up 1 time in 20.
  • Rolling two d20s and keeping the higher one (“advantage”) gives a 20 about 9.75% of the time.
  • A modifier just shifts the total: 1d20+5 ranges from 6 to 25.

Reading dice notation

NotationMeaningRange
1d6One six-sided die1–6
3d6Three six-sided dice added3–18
2d8+3Two eight-sided dice plus 35–19
1d100Percentile roll1–100

Common mistakes

  • The gambler’s fallacy: after three 1s in a row, a 1 is still exactly as likely next roll.
  • Thinking all totals are equal: with two or more dice, middle totals are much more common.

Fair rolls for games and classrooms

Board games, role-playing games and classroom probability lessons all need fair dice. An online roller is useful when dice are missing, when you need many dice at once, or when a game uses unusual dice such as a d12 or d100.

Teachers can use it to run quick experiments: roll 2d6 fifty times as a class, tally the totals, and compare the results with the probability table above. With more rolls, the results get closer to the expected pattern.

Dice myths versus the math

  • Myth: 3d6 and 1d16+2 are the same because both run from 3 to 18. Fact: With three dice, 10 and 11 each come up 12.5% of the time while 3 or 18 appear once in 216 rolls. A single d16 would give every total the same 6.25%.
  • Myth: Rolling with disadvantage (two d20, keep the lower) halves your chance of a 20. Fact: Both dice must show 20, so the chance falls from 5% to 0.25%, one roll in 400.
  • Myth: A +5 modifier makes high results more likely. Fact: It shifts every outcome up by 5; each of the 20 totals from 6 to 25 still has a 5% chance.
  • Myth: Three sixes in a row prove a die is loaded. Fact: On a fair d6 that streak is 1 in 216, so it will turn up a few times over a long campaign.
  • Myth: On percentile dice, 00 on the tens die and 0 on the ones die means zero. Fact: The usual convention reads that pair as 100.

Dice questions from game night

Can I use this for real-money gambling?
No. It is meant for games and teaching probability.

Why keep the last five rolls?
So everyone at the table can check what was rolled.

Is the online dice roller really random?
Yes. It uses the browser’s cryptographic random generator, so no number is favored.

What is a d20?
A 20-sided die, used for most checks in games like Dungeons & Dragons.

Related calculators

Percentage Calculator · GPA Calculator · Grade Calculator

For irregular rooms, split them into rectangles and add each one.

Planning new flooring, carpet, paint or tile? Measure each room, enter length and width in feet, and get the total square footage plus an estimated material cost.

Measuring a room the right way

Flooring, carpet, tile and paint are all priced by area, so a careful measurement can save real money. The rule is simple — length times width — but rooms are rarely perfect rectangles, and inches need to be turned into feet first.

How to use the square footage calculator

  1. Measure each room’s length and width in feet.
  2. Enter up to four areas.
  3. Add the price per square foot and a waste allowance if you like.
  4. Press Calculate.

The formula

Square feet = length (ft) × width (ft)  |  1 sq ft = 0.0929 m²

Worked example: two rooms of flooring

A 12 × 14 ft bedroom is 168 sq ft and a 10 × 11 ft office is 110 sq ft, for 278 sq ft in total. With a 10% waste allowance you should buy about 306 sq ft. At $3.49 per sq ft, the material costs about $1,067. The same area is 25.8 m² or 30.9 square yards.

Case study: 278 square feet, sold 19.63 at a time

Flooring is rarely sold by the exact square foot. Laminate, vinyl plank and engineered wood come in cartons, and you can only buy whole ones. Take the two rooms from the example above, 278 sq ft, and a plank whose box label says it covers 19.63 sq ft.

  1. Add 10% waste: 278 × 1.10 = 305.8 sq ft.
  2. Divide by the carton coverage: 305.8 ÷ 19.63 = 15.6 cartons.
  3. Round up, never down: 16 cartons, covering 314.08 sq ft.
  4. Price it by the carton. At $2.99 per sq ft a carton costs $58.69, so 16 cartons come to about $939.

You end up with 36 sq ft more than the bare floor, about 13% extra. That is not wasted money: keep one unopened carton for repairs, because dye lots change. If the plank needs separate underlayment, it usually comes in 100 sq ft rolls, so this job takes three rolls.

Converting inches to feet

Divide the inches by 12 and add them to the feet. A wall that measures 11 ft 7 in is 11 + 7/12 = 11.58 ft. A room of 11 ft 7 in × 13 ft 2 in is 11.58 × 13.17 = about 152.5 sq ft.

InchesFeet (decimal)
3 in0.25
4 in0.33
6 in0.5
8 in0.67
9 in0.75

L-shaped and odd-shaped rooms

Split the floor into rectangles that do not overlap, measure each one and add them. The calculator has four rows for this. For a closet or bay window, measure it as its own small rectangle.

Waste allowance by job

MaterialTypical extra
Laminate or vinyl plank, straight layout5–10%
Tile, straight layout10%
Tile, diagonal or herringbone15–20%
Carpet5–10% (roll width matters)

Paint is measured on the walls

For paint, use the wall area: room perimeter × ceiling height. A 12 × 14 ft room with 8 ft walls has 2 × (12 + 14) × 8 = 416 sq ft of wall. Subtract roughly 20 sq ft for each door and 15 sq ft for each window. A gallon usually covers about 350–400 sq ft per coat, but check the can.

Common mistakes

  • Typing 11.7 for 11 ft 7 in — that is 11 ft 8.4 in. Convert inches first.
  • Forgetting waste and running short of the same dye lot.
  • Using square yards and square feet together: 1 square yard = 9 sq ft.

Why a listing's square footage is not your flooring number

A home listed at 1,500 sq ft will not need 1,500 sq ft of flooring. Listings and mortgage appraisals usually report gross living area under the ANSI Z765 standard, which measures differently from the way you measure a room:

  • It is taken from the outside of the exterior walls. A 30 × 50 ft footprint is 1,500 sq ft outside but about 29 × 49 = 1,421 sq ft inside 6-inch walls, before interior walls and closets come off.
  • Only finished space above grade counts. A finished basement is listed separately, and garages, porches and unfinished attics are left out.
  • Areas with ceilings under about 7 feet are excluded, which trims attic rooms with sloped ceilings.
  • Stairs are counted on the floor they descend from, not on the floor below.

Measured room by room, the floor you can actually cover is often 5 to 10% below the listed figure. Property tax records may use yet another method, so none of these numbers replaces a tape measure.

Reader questions about measuring rooms

How many square feet is a 12 × 12 room?
144 sq ft, or about 13.4 m².

Should I measure wall to wall or include the baseboard?
Measure wall to wall at floor level. The baseboard covers the small gap at the edges.

How do I convert inches to feet?
Divide inches by 12. For example, 10 ft 9 in = 10.75 ft.

How many square feet are in a square yard?
Nine. Carpet is often priced per square yard.

Related calculators

title: Fraction Calculator - Add, Subtract, Multiply and Divide Fractions
html:
Fraction Calculator

Enter two fractions
//

Use negative numbers in the top box for negative fractions. Results are simplified.

Fractions show up in homework, recipes and woodworking. Enter two fractions, choose an operation, and get a simplified answer plus the mixed number and decimal.

Working with fractions, step by step

Fractions trip people up because each operation has its own rule. The calculator does the arithmetic and simplifies the answer, but it helps to see why the result is right — especially when you are checking homework or cutting wood.

How to use the fraction calculator

  1. Type the top and bottom numbers of each fraction.
  2. Choose +, −, × or ÷.
  3. Press Calculate.

The formula

a/b + c/d = (ad + bc) ÷ bd  |  a/b × c/d = ac ÷ bd  |  a/b ÷ c/d = ad ÷ bc

Four worked examples

  • Add: 1/2 + 1/3. The common denominator is 6, so 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6.
  • Subtract: 5/6 − 1/4. Use 12 as the denominator: 10/12 − 3/12 = 7/12.
  • Multiply: 2/3 × 3/5 = 6/15, which simplifies to 2/5.
  • Divide: 3/4 ÷ 1/8 = 3/4 × 8/1 = 24/4 = 6. Six one-eighth pieces fit into three quarters.

Sixteenths on a U.S. tape measure

A U.S. tape measure splits each inch into 16 parts. The longest marks are inches, then halves, quarters, eighths and finally the short sixteenth marks. To read a length, count the small marks past the last whole inch: five marks past 7 is 7 5/16 in.

MarkDecimal inchesMillimeters
1/160.06251.59
1/80.1253.18
3/160.18754.76
1/40.256.35
3/80.3759.53
1/20.512.7

Adding two measurements means putting both in sixteenths: 7 5/16 + 3 7/8 = 117/16 + 62/16 = 179/16 = 11 3/16 in. Then remember the saw blade. A typical blade removes about 1/8 in, so cutting a 48 in board into two equal pieces gives 23 15/16 in each, not 24.

Mixed numbers in real life

The calculator takes simple fractions, so turn a mixed number into an improper fraction first: multiply the whole number by the denominator and add the numerator. 2 1/2 becomes 5/2 and 1 3/4 becomes 7/4. Then 5/2 + 7/4 = 10/4 + 7/4 = 17/4, shown as the mixed number 4 1/4.

Woodworking: a board is 5 3/8 inches and you cut off 2 7/16 inches. Enter 43/8 − 39/16. The answer is 47/16, or 2 15/16 inches left.

Recipes: making a recipe 1.5 times bigger? Multiply 3/4 cup by 3/2 to get 9/8 — that is 1 1/8 cups.

Least common denominators you will meet often

FractionsCommon denominatorRewritten
1/2 and 1/363/6 and 2/6
1/4 and 1/6123/12 and 2/12
3/8 and 5/16166/16 and 5/16
2/3 and 3/4128/12 and 9/12
1/5 and 1/10102/10 and 1/10

Common mistakes

  • Adding the bottoms: 1/2 + 1/3 is not 2/5. Denominators only stay the same, they are never added.
  • Forgetting to flip when dividing: dividing by 1/8 is the same as multiplying by 8.
  • Losing the minus sign: put a negative sign on the top number only, such as −3/4.
  • Not simplifying: 6/15 and 2/5 are equal, but most teachers expect the simplest form.

Five ways to tell which fraction is bigger

Which is larger, 5/8 or 11/16? Work down this list and stop at the first rule that applies.

  1. Same denominator: compare the tops. 7/12 is bigger than 5/12.
  2. Same numerator: the smaller bottom wins, because its pieces are larger. 3/5 is bigger than 3/8.
  3. Benchmark against one half: 7/15 is under a half (half of 15 is 7.5) and 9/17 is over it (half of 17 is 8.5), so 9/17 is bigger.
  4. Cross-multiply: for a/b against c/d, compare a × d with c × b. For 5/8 and 11/16: 5 × 16 = 80 and 11 × 8 = 88, so 11/16 is bigger.
  5. Convert to decimals when the denominators are awkward: 7/12 = 0.583 and 4/7 = 0.571, so 7/12 wins by about 0.012.

Rule 4 works every time; rules 1 to 3 are faster in your head and a good check on any answer the tool gives you.

Fraction questions students and DIYers ask

Why does the calculator show a decimal too?
Decimals are easier to compare. 5/6 = 0.833333, which is a little more than 4/5 = 0.8.

Can I use the common denominator a × b every time?
Yes, multiplying the two denominators always works, but the answer then needs more simplifying. The least common denominator keeps the numbers small.

What is an improper fraction?
A fraction whose top is larger than its bottom, such as 17/4. It equals the mixed number 4 1/4.

How do I simplify a fraction?
Divide the top and bottom by their greatest common factor. 12/16 ÷ 4 = 3/4.

How do I enter a mixed number?
Convert it first: 2 1/2 = (2 × 2 + 1)/2 = 5/2.

Related calculators

Percentage Calculator · Grade Calculator · GPA Calculator

Sources and further reading

  • Khan Academy – Arithmetic: fractions, decimals and comparing fractions
  • NIST Office of Weights and Measures – inch to millimeter conversion (1 in = 25.4 mm)

title: Debt Snowball vs Avalanche Calculator - Find Your Fastest Way Out of Debt
html:
Debt Snowball vs Avalanche

Your debts (leave unused rows empty)
NameBalance $APR %Min. pay $
Extra money per month (on top of all minimum payments)
$

Snowball pays the smallest balance first; avalanche pays the highest APR first. Freed-up payments roll into the next debt.

If you have several debts — credit cards, a car loan, student loans — the order you pay them off matters. This calculator compares the two most popular strategies, the debt snowball and the debt avalanche, using your real numbers.

Snowball or avalanche: which one should you use?

Both methods have the same basic rule: pay the minimum on every debt, then put every extra dollar toward one target debt. When that debt is gone, roll its payment into the next one. The only difference is the order. The snowball targets the smallest balance first; the avalanche targets the highest interest rate first.

How to use the debt payoff calculator

  1. Enter each debt’s balance, APR and minimum payment.
  2. Enter any extra money you can add each month.
  3. Press Compare Methods to see payoff time, interest and order for both strategies.

The formula

Pay all minimums → put every extra dollar on one target debt → when it is gone, roll its payment into the next one

Worked example with $300 extra each month

Three debts: a store card of $1,500 at 12% (minimum $40), a credit card of $6,000 at 24% (minimum $150) and a car loan of $9,000 at 6% (minimum $280).

MethodDebt-free inTotal interestFirst debt gone
Minimums only≈ 48 months≈ $5,610month 36
Snowball≈ 25 months≈ $2,200month 5
Avalanche≈ 24 months≈ $1,980month 16

The avalanche saves about $220 here, but the snowball delivers its first win in month 5 instead of month 16. Both are dramatically better than paying minimums — the extra $300 is what does most of the work.

What the minimum payment warning box is telling you

Since the Credit CARD Act of 2009, every monthly credit card statement must show two things: how long it would take to clear the balance paying only the minimum, and the monthly amount that would clear it in 36 months. That box is a one-debt version of this tool, so it is worth reading.

Take the $6,000 card at 24% from the example above. Many issuers set the minimum at 1% of the balance plus that month's interest, with a floor of around $25. Paying only that:

  • The first payment is about $180 ($60 toward the balance, $120 of interest).
  • Each payment shrinks as the balance falls, so the balance barely moves in later years.
  • The card takes roughly 21 years to clear and costs about $10,900 in interest.

The 36-month figure on the same statement would be about $235 a month, for roughly $2,470 in interest. Enter $235 as that card's payment here to see how much the whole stack speeds up.

How to choose

  • Choose avalanche if your high-rate debt is large and you are motivated by numbers. It always costs the least.
  • Choose snowball if you have several small balances or have tried and stopped before. Quick wins keep many people going.
  • A hybrid works too: clear one or two tiny balances first, then switch to the highest rate.

Tips that make either method work

  • Keep the total monthly amount the same even as debts disappear — that is the "snowball".
  • Put windfalls (tax refunds, bonuses) toward the target debt.
  • Don't take on new debt while paying off old debt; consider freezing cards you are paying down.

Four checks before moving a balance to a 0% card

  1. Price the transfer fee against the interest. A 3% fee on $6,000 is $180; at 24% APR that balance costs about $120 in interest in the first month alone, so the fee is repaid in under two months.
  2. Divide the new balance by the promo months. $6,180 over an 18-month 0% period needs $343 a month. If you cannot commit to that, whatever is left rolls onto the regular rate.
  3. Confirm it is a true 0% APR, not deferred interest. Store financing that says "no interest if paid in full" charges all the back interest if even $1 remains when the promotion ends. Credit card balance-transfer offers normally do not.
  4. Keep new purchases off the transfer card. New charges may lose their grace period while a transferred balance is open. In the tool, enter the transferred debt at 0% with the $343 payment and let the avalanche target your remaining high-rate cards.

What readers ask about paying off debt

Should mortgages be included?
Most people leave the mortgage out and focus on consumer debt first, because mortgage rates are usually lower and the term is long.

What if two debts have the same rate?
Pay the smaller one first; you free up its minimum sooner.

Is debt consolidation better?
It can be, if the consolidation loan has a lower APR and you don't run up the cards again. Run the loan calculator to compare.

Which is better, snowball or avalanche?
Avalanche always costs the same or less interest. Snowball can feel more motivating because small debts disappear quickly.

Should I include my mortgage?
Usually no. Most people focus on consumer debt first and keep the mortgage on its normal schedule.

Related calculators

Credit Card Payoff · Loan Calculator

Sources and further reading

  • CFPB – Credit cards (statement disclosures, balance transfers, deferred interest)
  • MyMoney.gov – federal financial literacy resources on managing debt

Payoff timelines assume fixed rates and on-time payments; your card agreement and a qualified counselor decide what applies to you.

title: Loan Calculator - Monthly Payment, Total Interest and Amortization Schedule
html:
Loan Calculator

Loan amount
$
Interest rate
% per year
Loan term
yearsmonths

Fixed-rate loan with equal monthly payments (amortized). Estimates only.

Whether it is a personal loan, student loan or small business loan, the first question is always the same: how much will I pay each month, and how much interest in total? This loan calculator answers both and shows a yearly amortization schedule.

How to read your loan results

A personal loan, student loan or small business loan is usually repaid in equal monthly installments. Each payment covers that month's interest first, and whatever is left reduces the balance. Because the balance shrinks, the interest part gets smaller every month and the principal part gets larger. The amortization schedule in this calculator shows that shift month by month, so you can see exactly where your money goes.

How to use the loan calculator

  1. Enter the amount you want to borrow.
  2. Enter the annual interest rate (APR).
  3. Enter the term in years and months.
  4. Press Calculate.

The formula

Payment = L × r ÷ (1 − (1 + r)−n)

The two numbers that matter most

The monthly payment tells you whether the loan fits your budget. The total interest tells you what the loan really costs. A longer term lowers the first number but raises the second, and that trade-off is the most important decision you make when borrowing.

Worked case: the fee that hides inside the APR

The example above borrows $20,000 at 9% for 60 months, giving a payment of $415.17. Now suppose the lender charges a 5% origination fee. Two things can happen, and you can model both here.

  • Fee taken from the proceeds. You receive $19,000 but repay $415.17 a month on $20,000. The yearly cost on the money you actually got works out to about 11.2%, which is close to the APR the lender must disclose under the Truth in Lending Act.
  • Fee added to the loan. To net $20,000 you borrow $21,053. The payment rises to about $437 and total interest to about $5,170, up from $4,910.

Either way the fee costs you roughly $1,000 plus interest on it. A no-fee loan at 10% ($425 a month, $5,496 in interest) is the cheaper deal in both cases. When offers are close, compare APRs rather than note rates, and ask whether the fee is deducted or financed.

Worked example: $20,000 at 9%

TermMonthly paymentTotal interest
3 years (36 months)≈ $636≈ $2,896
5 years (60 months)≈ $415≈ $4,910

Stretching the same loan from three to five years saves about $221 a month, but costs roughly $2,000 more in interest. If the shorter payment is comfortable, it is usually the cheaper choice. If cash flow is tight, the longer term with occasional extra payments gives you both safety and savings.

Why the rate you are offered can differ

  • Credit score – the single biggest factor for unsecured loans.
  • Debt-to-income ratio – lenders compare your monthly debt payments with your gross income.
  • Fees – an origination fee of 1–8% is often taken out of the loan amount. Compare offers by APR, which includes these fees.
  • Secured vs unsecured – a loan backed by a car or savings account is usually cheaper.

Paying extra: what actually happens

Most installment loans let you pay extra toward principal without penalty. Every extra dollar reduces the balance that interest is charged on, so the savings compound. On the 5-year example above, adding $50 a month shortens the loan by about 7 months and saves several hundred dollars. Before paying extra, check the loan agreement for a prepayment penalty and ask the lender to apply the money to principal, not to next month's payment.

Common mistakes

  • Comparing only monthly payments between offers with different terms.
  • Ignoring the origination fee: a $20,000 loan with a 5% fee only puts $19,000 in your account.
  • Borrowing for longer than the thing you are buying lasts.

Quick reminders

  • Even a 1% lower rate can save hundreds or thousands of dollars.

Federal student loan, personal loan or auto loan: what differs

The amortization math is the same for all three, but the terms behind the numbers are not alike.

FeatureFederal Direct student loanPersonal loanAuto loan
Who sets the rateFixed by federal formula each July 1, same for every borrower in a categoryLender, from credit score and incomeLender, from credit and the car's age
Credit checkNone for undergraduate Direct loansYesYes
CollateralNoneNoneThe vehicle; lender holds the title
Typical term10 years standard, longer on income-driven plans2 to 7 years3 to 7 years
If income dropsDeferment, forbearance and income-driven plans by lawHardship options at the lender's discretionFew; missed payments risk repossession

The practical rule: use federal student aid before private borrowing for school, finance a car for no longer than you expect to keep it, and treat an unsecured personal loan as the most expensive of the three unless your credit is strong.

Borrowers' questions, answered

Is this the same formula banks use?
Yes. Fixed-rate installment loans use the standard amortization formula: payment = P × r ÷ (1 − (1 + r)−n), where r is the monthly rate and n the number of months.

Why is my first payment different?
Interest is charged by the day, so a first period longer or shorter than a month changes the first payment slightly.

Should I consolidate several debts into one loan?
Only if the new APR is clearly lower and you stop adding to the old balances. See the debt snowball and credit card payoff calculators to compare.

What is amortization?
Amortization means each equal payment covers that month’s interest first and the rest pays down the balance, so the interest part shrinks over time.

Does this include fees?
No. Origination fees or insurance are not included. Add them to the loan amount if they are financed.

Related calculators

Credit Card Payoff · Debt Snowball vs Avalanche · Auto Loan

Sources and further reading

  • Federal Student Aid – Direct Loan rates, fees and repayment plans
  • CFPB – Auto loans (shopping, terms and what lenders can do)

How we checked this page: example figures were recomputed with the standard amortization formula. Background reading: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau guides on personal loans (consumerfinance.gov). Last reviewed November 2026. General information only, not financial advice. Payments shown are for fixed-rate loans without fees; real offers vary, so read the Truth in Lending disclosure before signing.

title: Inflation Calculator - Future Cost and Purchasing Power of Money
html:
Inflation Calculator

What do you want to know?
Amount today
$
Average inflation rate
% per year
Years
years

Uses a constant average inflation rate. Actual inflation changes from year to year.

Inflation slowly raises prices and shrinks what your money can buy. Use this calculator to see what things will cost in the future, or how much your savings will really be worth.

What inflation does to your money over time

Inflation is the general rise in prices. When it runs at 3% a year, something that costs $100 today costs about $103 next year. Over long periods the effect compounds just like interest, which is why it matters so much for retirement planning, salaries and long-term savings.

How to use the inflation calculator

  1. Choose future cost or future value of money.
  2. Enter the amount, an average inflation rate and the number of years.
  3. Press Calculate.

The formula

Future cost = today’s price × (1 + inflation)years  |  future value = amount ÷ (1 + inflation)years

Worked example

At 3% a year for 20 years, prices rise by a factor of about 1.81. Something that costs $100 today would cost roughly $181. Seen the other way, $100,000 saved in cash today would buy only what about $55,400 buys now. By the Rule of 72, prices double in about 72 ÷ 3 = 24 years.

Inflation rate$100 after 10 years$100 after 20 years
2%≈ $122≈ $149
3%≈ $134≈ $181
4%≈ $148≈ $219

Which price index adjusts your benefits, taxes and bonds

"Inflation" in the news usually means the CPI-U, but several official indexes exist and each one drives a different part of your finances.

IndexPublished byWhat it adjusts
CPI-U (all urban consumers)Bureau of Labor StatisticsHeadline inflation; Series I savings bond rates; many rent and contract escalators
CPI-W (wage earners)Bureau of Labor StatisticsSocial Security cost-of-living adjustment, from the third-quarter average
Chained CPI (C-CPI-U)Bureau of Labor StatisticsFederal income tax brackets and the standard deduction
Core CPIBureau of Labor StatisticsCPI without food and energy; used to read the trend, not to index payments
PCE price indexBureau of Economic AnalysisThe Federal Reserve's 2% target

The gaps between them look small, often a few tenths of a point a year, but they compound: an index that runs 0.3 points lower for 30 years ends about 8.5% lower, one reason the chained CPI was chosen for tax brackets. When you set a rate here, match it to the money you are planning: CPI-W for Social Security, CPI-U for almost everything else.

Real vs nominal returns

If your savings earn 4% but inflation is 3%, your purchasing power grows by only about 1%. This "real" return is what matters for long-term goals. Money in a checking account earning nothing loses value every year.

Where inflation shows up in planning

  • Salary: a 3% raise in a year of 3% inflation keeps you even, not ahead.
  • Retirement: estimate future expenses in today's dollars, then grow them with inflation.
  • Big goals: college costs and healthcare have often risen faster than overall inflation.

A fixed $2,000 pension after 10, 20 and 30 years

Social Security rises with inflation, but most private pensions and fixed annuities pay the same dollar amount for life. Here is what a $2,000 monthly check buys in today's dollars, using the future-value mode above.

Years from nowAt 2.5% inflationAt 3% inflation
10$1,562$1,488
20$1,221$1,107
30$953$824

After 20 years at 3%, you would need $3,612 a month to match today's $2,000. The planning rule that follows: treat a fixed pension as covering a shrinking share of expenses, and let inflation-adjusted income or growing investments cover the rest. If a pension offers a cost-of-living rider in exchange for a lower starting payment, run both versions here before choosing.

Inflation questions from savers and retirees

What rate should I use?
The U.S. Federal Reserve targets 2% over the long run; many planners use 2.5–3% to be cautious.

Where do official figures come from?
The Consumer Price Index (CPI) published by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (bls.gov).

What has US inflation averaged?
Over the past century US consumer prices have risen about 3% a year on average, with big swings in some decades.

Where can I find official inflation data?
The US Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes the Consumer Price Index (CPI) every month at bls.gov.

Related calculators

Compound Interest · Retirement Calculator

Sources and further reading

  • Bureau of Labor Statistics – Consumer Price Index (CPI-U, CPI-W, chained CPI)
  • Social Security Administration – Retirement benefits and cost-of-living adjustments
  • Federal Reserve – monetary policy and the 2% inflation goal

title: Date Calculator - Days Between Dates and Add or Subtract Days
html:
Date Calculator

What do you want to do?
Start date
End date
Days
days

Calendar days, including weekends and holidays.

How many days until a trip, a wedding or a deadline? What date is 90 days from today? This date calculator answers both in one click.

Counting days between dates the right way

"How many days until…" sounds simple, but calendars have months of 28 to 31 days and leap years every four years (with exceptions). This calculator counts actual calendar days, and can also add or subtract days from a date — useful for deadlines, notice periods, travel and countdowns.

How to use the date calculator

  1. Choose “Days between two dates” or “Add or subtract days”.
  2. Pick the dates (today is pre-selected).
  3. Press Calculate.

The formula

Days = end date − start date (add 1 to include both days)

Worked examples

  • From January 1, 2026 to December 25, 2026 is 358 days.
  • 90 days after November 14, 2026 is February 12, 2027.
  • 30 days before March 1, 2027 is January 30, 2027 (February 2027 has 28 days).

Federal holidays that stretch a business-day count

The weekday count above skips Saturdays and Sundays but not holidays, because holidays differ by state, employer and bank. For federal deadlines and most banks, subtract these 11 federal holidays when they fall inside your range:

  • New Year's Day (Jan 1), Martin Luther King Jr. Day (third Monday in January), Washington's Birthday (third Monday in February)
  • Memorial Day (last Monday in May), Juneteenth (June 19), Independence Day (July 4)
  • Labor Day (first Monday in September), Columbus Day (second Monday in October), Veterans Day (Nov 11)
  • Thanksgiving (fourth Thursday in November), Christmas Day (Dec 25)

A fixed-date holiday that falls on Saturday is observed on Friday; one that falls on Sunday moves to Monday. Example: 10 business days from Friday, November 20, 2026 is Monday, December 7, because Thanksgiving on November 26 drops out. Fourteen calendar days would end on December 4. For federal tax filings, a due date that lands on a weekend or legal holiday moves to the next business day.

Inclusive or exclusive?

Most calculators, including this one, don't count the start date: from Monday to Tuesday is 1 day. If you need to count both ends — for example, a hotel stay counted in days instead of nights, or "a 7-day course from the 1st to the 7th" — add 1 to the result.

Calendar days vs business days

Many legal and banking deadlines use business days, which skip weekends and public holidays. A "10 business day" refund can take two full weeks or more. Count calendar days here, then subtract weekends and holidays if your deadline uses business days.

Leap years

A year is a leap year if it is divisible by 4, except century years, which must be divisible by 400. So 2028 is a leap year, 2100 is not, and 2000 was. The calculator includes February 29 automatically.

Handy reference

PeriodDays
4 weeks28
13 weeks (a quarter)91
Common year / leap year365 / 366

90 days and three months are not the same

Contracts, leases and medical follow-ups mix the two. Adding three months keeps the same day of the month (clamped to the last day if the month is shorter), while 90 days is a fixed count. The results can differ by a day or more:

Start datePlus 90 daysPlus 3 months
Nov 30, 2026Feb 28, 2027Feb 28, 2027
Jan 31, 2027May 1, 2027Apr 30, 2027
Jun 1, 2026Aug 30, 2026Sep 1, 2026
Dec 1, 2027Feb 29, 2028Mar 1, 2028
Jul 1, 2026Dec 28, 2026 (180 days)Jan 1, 2027 (6 months)

If a document says "90 days", use the add-days mode; if it says "three months", count on the calendar. When money or rights depend on it, ask which one the other party means and get it in writing.

Date questions we hear most

Is "3 months" the same as 90 days?
No. Three calendar months can be 89 to 92 days. Check which your contract uses.

How do I count business days?
The result shows weekdays (Monday to Friday). Subtract any public holidays in that range.

What date is 100 days from today?
Choose “Add or subtract days”, keep today as the start date and enter 100.

Related calculators

Age Calculator · Hours Calculator · Due Date Calculator

Sources and further reading

  • IRS – filing due dates that fall on weekends and legal holidays

title: Compound Interest Calculator - See How Your Savings Grow with Monthly Deposits
html:
Compound Interest Calculator

Initial deposit
$
Monthly contribution
$
Annual interest rate
%
Years
years
Compounding

Contributions are added at the end of each month. Taxes and fees are not included.

Compound interest means you earn interest on your interest. Given enough time, it turns small regular savings into a large balance. See how your money can grow with this calculator.

How compound interest really works

With simple interest you earn only on what you deposited. With compound interest, the interest you earned is added to the balance and starts earning interest too. The effect is small in the first years and very large later — which is why time matters more than almost anything else in saving.

How to use the compound interest calculator

  1. Enter what you start with and what you will add each month.
  2. Enter the expected annual return or interest rate.
  3. Enter the number of years and choose how often interest compounds.
  4. Press Calculate.

The formula

A = P × (1 + r/k)k×t + monthly contributions growing the same way

Worked example: $10,000 plus $300 a month at 7%

After 20 years, monthly compounding grows the account to about $196,700. You put in $82,000 yourself ($10,000 plus $300 × 240 months); the other $114,700 is growth. In the last few years, the account earns more each year than you contribute.

Annual rateYears to double (Rule of 72)
3%≈ 24
6%≈ 12
8%≈ 9
10%≈ 7.2

Case study: $300 a month from age 25 versus age 35

Two savers each put $300 a month into an account earning 7% compounded monthly and stop at 65. The only difference is when they start.

  • Starts at 35 (30 years, $108,000 deposited): about $366,000 at 65.
  • Starts at 25 (40 years, $144,000 deposited): about $787,000 at 65.

The early saver deposits $36,000 more but ends with roughly $421,000 more. For the late starter to catch up by 65, the monthly deposit would have to be about $645, more than double. The reason is that the earliest deposits spend 30 to 40 years compounding: at 7% with monthly compounding, a dollar left alone for 40 years grows to about $16, while a dollar given 30 years grows to about $8. Try the same comparison at 5%; the gap narrows, but the early start still wins by a wide margin.

Three levers you control

  • Start earlier – ten extra years can matter more than a higher contribution.
  • Contribute regularly – automatic monthly deposits remove the need to decide each month.
  • Keep costs low – a 1% yearly fee can take a large share of long-term growth.

Be realistic about the rate

Savings accounts and CDs pay a known rate. Stock and bond returns are not guaranteed and vary year to year; long-run averages are only a guide. Try a lower rate too, and remember inflation: a 7% return with 3% inflation is about 4% in real purchasing power.

Five things to check before chasing a higher rate

  1. Is the account insured? FDIC coverage at banks and NCUA coverage at credit unions each protect up to $250,000 per depositor, per institution, per ownership category. Money market mutual funds, stocks and bonds are not insured.
  2. Is the number an APY? Compare APY with APY. A 5% rate compounded daily is 5.13% APY; compounded monthly it is 5.12%.
  3. Is it a promotional rate? Note the end date and the rate it drops to, and plan to move the money if the new rate is weak.
  4. Do fees eat the interest? A $5 monthly fee on a $2,000 balance at 4% APY takes $60 of the $80 earned, leaving a net return of 1%.
  5. What is left after tax? Interest in an ordinary account is reported on Form 1099-INT and taxed as income. In the 22% bracket, 4.5% becomes about 3.5% after tax, which is why retirement accounts feature in long-term examples.

Savings growth questions, answered

Does compounding frequency matter?
A little. Daily versus monthly compounding changes results only slightly; the rate and the number of years matter far more.

What about taxes?
Interest in a regular account is usually taxed each year, which slows growth. Retirement accounts can defer or avoid that tax.

Is the Rule of 72 exact?
It's a quick estimate that is most accurate between about 6% and 10%.

What is APY?
APY is the yearly return including compounding. A 5% rate compounded monthly equals about 5.12% APY.

Is 7% a realistic return?
Over long periods the US stock market has averaged roughly 7% after inflation, but returns vary a lot year to year and are not guaranteed.

Related calculators

Retirement Calculator · Inflation Calculator

Sources and further reading

  • Investor.gov (SEC) – Compound Interest Calculator
  • IRS – reporting interest income (Form 1099-INT)
